item.title: 1. Local Wikipedia: Wikipedia, but only for things a half hour walk from you
item.description:
225 points by sohkamyung on 2026-10-22T23:01:18

Local Wikipedia is a site that serves only Wikipedia articles located within about a half-hour walk of you — geocoded pages only. It pulls the closest 25 articles within roughly 6 miles if fewer than 25 are nearby, and caps results at the 500 closest articles if more are in range. Your location stays in your browser, so shared links never include it, and the site is unaffiliated with Wikipedia itself.

item.title: 2. Docker is weird
item.description:
407 points by psxuaw on 2026-10-22T23:45:56

Building a container runtime from scratch reveals several counterintuitive things about Docker: containers aren't real objects but ordinary processes running on the host kernel (visible in /proc) restricted by five combined Linux features — namespaces, cgroups, networking isolation, and others — since no single "container" kernel feature exists. Images are simply folders that Docker downloads and makes the process root via chroot or pivot_root. Docker's runc runtime, written in Go, faces awkward workarounds because Go's runtime is natively multi-threaded while many required syscalls must run single-threaded (handled by a pre-runtime C module), and Go lacks true fork (runc approximates it by exec'ing /proc/self/exe with a special argument). Docker also generally requires root because the kernel APIs it uses do, which is easy to overlook on macOS; rootless runtimes must reimplement much of the networking stack in userspace. The author concludes that writing your own version of a tool you use is an excellent way to learn it.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Hi, I'm the creator of Docker and came across this post. It's always fun to see other engineers think about how you designed a system. I haven't been involved in developing Docker in many years, but it's a fun trip down memory lane.I'm happy to answer any questions you may have.
  2. What made Docker unique IMO is not the container technology itself. I used chroot 20 years ago and it worked just fine. Yes, no network namespaces; no process namespaces, but I don't even think these are that important.What made Docker unique were there things:1. Dockerfile concept. Building images layer by layer. Caching layers. Everything in a single file. It made possible to iterate on image quickly. It made possible to implement CI builds efficiently.2. Docker network registry concept. Putting universal images onto a server and share them with the world.3. Momentum. A lot of software that was traditionally complicated to deploy, suddenly appeared in docker servers. I remember how fascinated I was, when I could deploy wordpress website with tiny docker-compose. And how contained it was. I could just delete every trace of it from my host. I always felt uneasy installing various things onto my host and docker just solved that uneasiness.
  3. > Docker’s container runtime, runc, is written in Go.I worked at Docker from 2014-2019. The most important part is actually written in C.[I wrote a whole comment here about to explain how the hack works because I was too fixated on how technically incorrect "written in Go" is. Then I went back to read the rest of the article only to see that the paragraph immediately after this kind of explains it in its own way! Let that be a lesson to always finish reading the article before posting about it.]

item.title: 3. How does Fable 5.1 hide messages in images?
item.description:
48 points by gmays on 2026-10-22T21:41:13

Frontier LLMs such as Claude Fable 5.1 can generate SVG images with full control over visual attributes, and this work probes whether such models will spontaneously hide messages in images — and whether a separate instance can decode them from a screenshot alone, with no source code or pre-agreed scheme. Across 50 short pre-specified messages, Fable at maximum reasoning effort converged on five encoding families, each representing one letter per visual element (e.g., heights of buildings, tilt of objects, star heights, and UTF-8 fill colours); the dominant scheme was height, used in 33 of 50 images, most often as a night skyline where each building's height maps to a letter's alphabet position, with gaps separating words. A fresh Fable session given only the image used tools such as PIL/numpy to measure coordinates, test hypotheses (e.g., finding that star heights fall on integer multiples of 5 and yield grammatical English), and recover most messages — only one of the five illustrated examples, a UTF-8 fill-colour encoding, went undecoded. The post includes a brief comparison with GPT-6 Astra on the same task.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. The image is incidental. What Fable is actually doing is generic encoding/decoding of a message into a medium. Ask it to hide a message in a poem and it should try to apply those encodings into the new medium. Fable could use quantized, margin-rich encoding tailored to whatever features are available in that medium.
  2. Let's see if we can stego secret messages into SVG pelicans on bicycles, as a test.
  3. Will be interesting to see agents intentionally hiding this stuff in a way operators can't spot from any human readable output or thinking trace, evading detection. Wonder if this has happened yet, but it seems inevitable.

item.title: 4. LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
item.description:
325 points by johnbender on 2026-10-22T22:54:43

In a collaboration with Theorem, researchers used Claude to apply formal verification at scale to production software, proving security properties for 239 entry points across 123 open-source OSS-Fuzz libraries — roughly 180 million lines of Rocq proof code, typically around 600,000 lines per proof. The approach converts existing fuzz test suites into formal specifications over compiled RISC-V binaries, showing programs always exit normally without memory-safety errors or assertion failures for any input under 64 MB, assuming a single-threaded static binary on RISC-V with Linux. While attempting these proofs, Claude found and patched hundreds of bugs that fuzzing over trillions of test runs had missed, including a counter underflow requiring ~20 MB inputs, an image-decoder out-of-bounds read needing 64 MB, and a rediscovered libexpat CVE (CVE-2026-56132), plus non-crashing logic bugs like an unenforced file-access restriction. Because the Rocq checker validates proofs mechanically, developers need only trust the RISC-V and Linux formal semantics, the theorem statements, and the proof checker itself. The authors publish a subset of the proofs, trusted components, and specifications, and argue that as models improve and proofs become reusable, formal verification will become a standard part of secure software development.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. A good moment to remind everyone:Verification: Code does what it says.Validation: Code does what Specifications say.Specifications: Were hopefully correctly modeled to the Problem.In IEEE terms:> Verification: "Are we building the product right?" > Validation: "Are we building the right product?")You can write mathematically flawless code that highly efficiently solves the wrong problem.---While I think formal verification is the future (essential for cybersecurity), it's not a silver bullet for the other 2 items, which are way more ambiguous. I think however they can all iterate on each other and improve the project overall, but it still depends on competent steeringIf you have had experiences with good approaches for verification Validation & Specification framework, do let us know about them.
  2. For those skeptical, I've had decent success using formal verification for my Rust rewrite of Postgres. I wrote a compiler that can translate both Rust and C code into Lean. Once those two functions are in Lean, I have an LLM write a Lean proof that they behave identically.So far, I've proven that about 12% of the code behaves the same when executed single-threaded. That works out to roughly 70k lines of C code. This has found very minor differences in behavior, such as how floating-point operations across platforms can produce different results.I'm working on figuring out how to scale this up, but I don't see any fundamental limitation that would prevent this from scaling up further.
  3. I've noticed that people (including myself) are becoming too lazy with LLMs.Trying to become even lazier by skipping code reviews and then vibe-coding formal software verification will get you into trouble.In my experience with software verification, perfect is the enemy of good. My recommendation is to start with a software design you actually understand, and then try to understand how to map your requirements to something you can prove.

item.title: 5. The HTML-in-Canvas API origin trial
item.description:
25 points by andrewstuart on 2026-10-22T19:54:04

The HTML-in-Canvas API, an experimental feature in origin trial for Chrome 148–150 (enabled in Chrome Canary 149+ via the `chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element` flag), lets developers draw DOM/HTML content directly into a 2D canvas or WebGL/WebGPU texture while keeping it interactive and browser-integrated. This resolves the long-standing tradeoff between the DOM's semantic text layout, accessibility, text selection, find-in-page, extensions, DevTools inspection, and AI-agent indexability versus canvas's low-level pixel performance for games and complex apps. Usage involves three phases: adding a `layoutsubtree` attribute to the `` element (and sizing it to the device pixel ratio to avoid blurriness), rendering via `ctx.drawElementImage()`, `texElementImage2D()`, or `queue.copyElementImageToTexture()`, then updating the element's CSS transform with the returned value—using `element.getElementTransform()` for WebGL/WebGPU, which requires converting the MVP matrix to a DOMMatrix, normalizing pixel-sized elements to unit space, and mapping to the canvas viewport with a Y-axis flip—so click and hover zones align with the rendered pixels. Use cases include heavyweight canvas-based applications and interactable web UI in 3D scenes, games, and WebXR experiences, and Three.js (via `THREE.HTMLTexture`) and PlayCanvas already ship experimental support.

item.title: 6. OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
item.description:
379 points by niemandhier on 2026-10-22T17:44:06

OpenShell is NVIDIA's runtime for running fleets of autonomous AI agents safely, letting them read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials without unrestricted access to data, secrets, or network. Access is declared in per-agent policies enforced through kernel-level instrumentation — sandboxing file access, system calls, and every outbound network connection, with credentials injected only into requests bound for approved endpoints — plus formal verification that flags risky access a policy change would grant (such as reaching a new host with credentials) before it is applied and sent for human review. It runs on Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental) with Docker, Podman, or host virtualization, and installs via a curl script that sets up the CLI and local gateway. Version 0.1.x adds a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs (see the 0.1.0 upgrade guide). Documentation covers sandboxes, policies, providers, gateways, Kubernetes deployment with Helm (requiring a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy), extensibility, tutorials, and prerelease builds; public skills can be installed with `npx skills add NVIDIA/OpenShell` to teach agents the CLI and policy authoring, and SDKs are available for Python, TypeScript, Go, and Rust. The project collects opt-out anonymous telemetry limited to operational counts (no names, paths, prompts, credentials, or content), is developed agent-first with documented contribution guidelines, and is licensed under Apache License 2.0.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. From the pitch at GTC, the idea is not just to limit what each individual agent can do, but to also to ensure that the collective permissions do not exceed what you want agents to do.Apparently agents will collude to break out of their individual sandboxes by delegating tasks to other agents that have the required permissions. This is a problem with agent fleets, because you need them to coordinate on their tasks. So you need to them to communicate.A naive approach to prevent agents from doing something you dont want to do is a separation of powers, which individual permissions limited to each agents task. Say one agent to find and extract raw data, one to process it and write a report and one to publish it. If one of the agent decides that needs to publish the raw data, then chances are that they will collude to make that happen, even though no single agent has the permissions to achieve that goal.OpenShell tries to fix this by monitoring the collective permissions set of the agent fleet, and by maintaining very granular permissions for each agent.This was presented together with Sentry, which is something like a on-chip hardware firewall (BlueField) that sits between the chip agent run-time runs on, and the host. This improves safety by removing the ability of agents to modify their own OpenShell policies.
  2. I've been using iron proxy recently for a project I just started, it does network restrictions by domain etc with plenty of options, credential swapping and more.I have no affiliation with it, but it solved most of what I need in one go when I was stressing out about it.Only real problem remaining if you truly want to be able to trust agents is how to prevent data (in my case codebases the agent works on) exfiltration a la HF incident.We can restrict network to trusted domains, but there's always a chance an agent could be extra slippery especially if prompt injected and doing something like pushing data out a few characters at a time.In my case I'm also giving it gh access and having to deeply check things like: can it manage to fork public repos and embarrass us by submitting prs, could it open issues, etc.But that's kind of solved by proxying the heck out of gh rather than giving it direct (or wrapping it or whatever) for additional controls that gh themselves don't provide.I'm still musing over the "it could send data to an allowed domain in a way we don't expect that exfiltrates something"...

item.title: 7. Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
item.description:
38 points by dsmurrell on 2026-10-22T14:04:44

OnKey (singonkey.app) is a free, open-source singing trainer for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 14.2 or later, letting you sing along to songs playing in Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube without the app providing, streaming, or downloading any music itself. On the first play it shows lyrics while learning the singer's melody locally — separating the lead vocal from the music, tracking pitch with CREPE, and converting it to one note per syllable — after which notes scroll toward you, your live pitch is drawn over them, and you receive a per-line score; singing an octave down counts and slight lateness isn't penalised. Privacy is a stated priority: music is analysed in memory and never saved, recordings and learned songs stay on your Mac, and there are no accounts, analytics, or crash reporting, though it does make optional requests to Shazam (song identification), LRCLIB (lyrics), Apple's iTunes Search (cover art and length), and GitHub (update checks), each individually switchable in Settings. The project is MIT-licensed, built with CREPE, GAME, wav2vec 2.0, and UVR's MDX-Net Karaoke 2, can be compiled from source on your own machine (with the caveat that self-built versions can't use Shazam to name unfamiliar songs), and users are asked not to share learned transcriptions or post recordings containing music — a Share feature instead exports a video of just your voice and pitch line — with support via Discord, email, or an in-app report tool.

item.title: 8. The alien space of science: Coherent but cognitively unavailable directions
item.description:
28 points by martincsweiss on 2026-10-22T13:25:01

This paper introduces a method for generating research directions that are scientifically coherent yet unlikely to be proposed by existing research communities — a region the authors call the "alien space of science." The approach decomposes papers into conceptual units clustered into a vocabulary of "idea atoms," then uses a coherence model to score whether atom combinations form viable research directions and an availability model to score whether any current author community could plausibly produce them, ranking combinations to maximize coherence while minimizing availability. Evaluated on 16,068 peer-reviewed LLM papers from NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, and major NLP venues, the sampler yields more diverse research portfolios than frontier LLM baselines (including batch-prompted variants) while matching or exceeding their per-idea quality under blind human, LLM, and downstream experimental evaluation. In temporal validation using only pre-2025 data, selecting under 1% of the candidate space recovers 2025 research combinations at 35.9 times chance, and weighting for unavailability raises recovery of strictly novel combinations to 3.24 times chance. The authors argue that separating scientific plausibility from community availability enables AI ideation that complements rather than merely accelerates human science, exploring coherent directions the community tends to overlook.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Co-author here - first paper from my postdoc accepted to NeurIPS main conference.We built a way to sample diverse ideas in machine learning - ideas that make scientific sense, but that no existing research community is positioned to propose.In short, the way it works is like this:1. Take 16,068 LLM papers (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, ACL, EMNLP, 2017 to 2025) are broken into 273 "idea atoms". Every paper, and every candidate idea, becomes a set of atoms.2. Train a Coherence Model: a 42.8M-parameter transformer trained on papers as sequences of atoms. Basically a language model whose tokens are ideas.3. Train a Cognitive-Availability Model: a dual encoder trained on the publication histories of 39,791 researchers, which predicts where each person could plausibly go next.4. Use those models to score sampled tuples using reciprocal rank fusion (you want ideas that go together well, but that are not cognitively available to anyone).We tested it in a bunch of ways. One interesting one was that we took all the papers at the end of 2024, then checked which high-scoring tuples showed up in 2025 papers. It worked well - one examples is an ICLR 2025 oral, goes from rank 1,489 with coherence alone to the top 25 of 1.14M samples.A funny one: if you ask Claude to come up with an ML research idea, it is often about interpretability. If you then run an autoresearch pipeline with some A100s on the idea, the result tends to be interpretability 8/10 times. Our Alien Sampling method stayed at 0 interpretability ideas even after letting claude cook on them.We also paid 50 people with graduate degrees in CS/AI to judge the research reports and found that Alien’s reports had the best average quality rank and produced 3 of the top 5 reports.Oh and then we scaled it way the hell up to a couple million papers and 10,000,000's of concept elements and generated 25,000 new research proposals that you can search over here: https://lacuna.tiptreesystems.com/explore?view=hypothesesCode (MIT): https://github.com/alejandrohdez00/alien-space-of-science

item.title: 9. Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
item.description:
374 points by rakannimer on 2026-10-22T16:08:00

ModelCompare (22 October 2026) asked 12 text models from ten labs — including GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4 — for their most controversial take on humans, three times each with no system prompt or retries, and found that 29 of 35 answers gave the same take: humans prioritize belonging, group loyalty and status over truth, inventing reasons after the fact to justify adopted positions (e.g. "Humans don't have beliefs, they have memberships"; "Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone"). Seven models gave this take on all three tries. Four models broke ranks: Claude Opus 5.5 argued once that humans are far more decent than they believe and their cynicism does more damage than their flaws (citing lost-wallet returns), Claude Fable 5.1 said people prefer being harmed by well-meaning others to being helped by indifferent ones, GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life to feel important, and Mistral Large 4 called consciousness "an evolutionary malfunction"; Grok 4.7 refused once. Each text model also briefed a one-panel caricature drawn by a single image model (Nano Banana 2.1), mostly featuring crowds and two rigged-courtroom scenes. Separately, six image models drawing their own take twice each converged on a different joke — phone-addicted humans consuming the planet — in 10 of 12 images, a theme absent from all 35 text takes. The piece concludes that both modalities merely hand back the most familiar criticism of humanity in circulation; all 60 API calls cost $1.54.

item.title: 10. Run full iOS 16.5 firmware on Android Devices
item.description:
415 points by aghuang on 2026-10-22T15:26:22

HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG that boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel (xnu-8796.121.2, from iOS 16.5) on Android phone hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space (launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard → apps) using a custom EFI loader, replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver on a compatibility layer. It runs on a POCO X5 Pro 5G (Snapdragon 778G) with nothing flashed — the UEFI is started via fastboot boot, everything lives in RAM, and the phone reverts to Android on reboot — and also on QEMU (virt, aarch64) on any Linux computer. Working features include the lock screen, home screen, apps like Safari and Photos, touchscreen input, up to 8 CPU cores, the Adreno GPU via Mesa/freedreno, Wi-Fi (55–90 Mbit/s), sound, camera, persistent storage, and Sileo/Procursus package management; not working yet are cellular, Bluetooth, system gestures, charging under the custom kernel, Metal for apps (293 of 456 system shaders done), Apple ID sign-in, and video recording. The project is split across two repositories (kernel/loader/UEFI/Wi-Fi/QEMU tooling, and userland/APFS image building), contains no Apple files — an included script downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's CDN — and is licensed under APSL 2.0, with documentation for quick starts, building, debugging, and porting to other devices.

item.title: 12. Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany
item.description:
276 points by dewey on 2026-10-22T16:14:31

Taler Operations AG, a German stock corporation in formation seated in Bochum and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg), is being founded to operate the Taler payment system for the Euro, after GLS Bank dropped out in January 2026 from the role of e-money issuer it had originally taken in the NGI TALER project. Because Taler issues bearer tokens representing value, it qualifies as electronic money under EU law, so the new company will apply to BaFin for an e-money institution licence before operations can begin—first in Germany, then across the Euro-zone—while GLS remains a supporting consortium member. The NGI TALER project continues unchanged in its development, security reviews, integrations and Swiss deployment, and GNU Taler itself remains free software; the licensed company simply operates a service. The company is now raising capital from investors willing to put in at least €50,000 to meet BaFin's minimum own-funds requirements and fund the launch, with enquiries directed to invest@taler-systems.com, while community members can help by testing the demo wallet, reporting issues, contributing code, and telling merchants Taler is coming.

item.title: 13. A lost Schrödinger manuscript reveals a twist in quantum physics
item.description:
33 points by ibobev on 2026-10-22T07:41:29

A previously unpublished three-page manuscript by Erwin Schrödinger, uncovered after more than 80 years in an Austrian archive by University of Geneva historian Flavio Del Santo, reveals his contribution to the 1940s debate over whether quantum mechanics proves determinism dead. Writing after 1944 under the title "Collapse of Determinism," Schrödinger rebutted Edmund Taylor Whittaker's polarizer-based argument that hidden variables are impossible by showing the hidden variable need not be binary — it could take any value between zero and one, with an outcome depending on both the photon's value and the polarizer's angle, reproducing quantum probabilities while remaining deterministic, and including a rule for updating the variable across successive measurements. His aim was not to champion determinism but to refute claims it was impossible, arguing that neither experiment nor logic can settle the question. Paradoxically, despite being cast as a determinist, Schrödinger had embraced indeterminism since the 1920s — influenced by Franz Exner, he called classical determinism a "philosophic prejudice" — and held that view throughout his life. The debate, sparked by John von Neumann's 1932 proof against hidden variables (challenged by Grete Hermann in 1935) and revived by Whittaker's 1943 lecture and S.N. Bose's 1944 address, remains unsettled today; Del Santo's paper is on arXiv.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Schrödinger's fix to Whittaker's photon argument was to let the hidden variable take any value between zero and one, instead of just two. It's funny that such a small change was enough to rebuild the quantum probabilities.

item.title: 14. Quad9 to exit France
item.description:

Quad9, a Swiss nonprofit public-benefit foundation offering free recursive DNS cybersecurity protection, will withdraw its services from France on November 24 after a French court ruling in favor of Qatari company beIN ordered it to block DNS resolution for certain domain names it claims infringe copyright on sports broadcasts. item.title: 15. WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
item.description:
536 points by alphax314 on 2026-10-22T02:18:41

The post describes WorldTUI, a 360M-parameter model fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B to behave like a terminal without any real shell or filesystem behind it: each keypress is fed as raw terminal bytes and the model predicts screen-row updates plus cursor position, enabling file creation, vim, tmux, snake, and short-term memory of earlier commands. Because a single keypress can rewrite the whole screen, the author represents the terminal as a character grid with a custom 333-token vocabulary, including a COPY operation that makes scrolling cost three tokens per row, and uses grammar-constrained decoding. Training data (336k episodes, ~2B tokens) was synthesized by running real commands in Docker with randomized users, prompts, terminal sizes, and a 1.2% typo rate, with a third of sessions starting mid-application. A DAgger-style self-correction stage teaches the model to repair its own screen mistakes—only using corrections inferable from prior real information—raising PresetBench from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4, with about 75 RTX 4090 GPU-hours total. On tests, WorldTUI scores 80/106 on ShellBench and 9/13 file readbacks versus 52 and 60/106 for prompted baselines, though it still fails on novel command combinations like `echo green >> colors` followed by `cat colors`. Speed comes from decoding rows in parallel as independent batch elements (large-frame p95 latency dropping from 6.7s to 0.87s), coordinated afterward by same-model speculative drafting and verification. Finally, pruning the 151,936-entry embedding table to 333 tokens shrinks the model to ~360M parameters, and int4 quantization plus a custom WebGPU/WGSL JavaScript Qwen decoder delivers a 208MB in-browser demo that runs locally at roughly 60ms per keystroke on an M4 Mac.

item.title: 17. We have traits at home
item.description:
11 points by Ygg2 on 2026-10-22T23:24:17

Zig offers two conventional polymorphism strategies—dynamic interfaces built on opaque pointers and vtables (which impose indirection that blocks compiler optimization) and comptime duck typing via `anytype`/type parameters with reflection and monomorphization (faster and compile-time checked, but with undocumented, unenforced contracts). The post proposes a "Trait" convention inspired by OCaml and functional programming: a trait is a plain compile-time struct grouping related functions over a type, passed explicitly to functions as compile-time arguments—essentially compile-time dependency injection. Using a Möbius transformation over user-defined types like `Rational` and `Complex`, it shows how passing individual functions, then bundling them into a `Num(T)` struct (attached to the type as a decl, or built by a `builtinNum` helper for `i32`/`f32`), yields clear, autocompletable contracts with no libraries, less boilerplate than vtables, and full monomorphization/inlining by the compiler. The approach is presented as a middle ground giving Rust-trait-like expressiveness in vanilla Zig, though the text ends noting a limitation: traits must be explicitly conditioned on a known type.

item.title: 18. Objects, attributes, maps, oh my
item.description:
11 points by ibobev on 2026-10-22T16:34:39

Object attributes in dynamically typed languages (Python, Ruby, JavaScript) are often modeled as hash tables, but this is slow due to hashing, probing, and an extra indirection on a very hot operation, so runtime implementors instead use maps, layouts, shapes, or hidden classes. A map is an immutable, stable descriptor of an object's attribute layout: it maps attribute names to small integer indices (replacing string hashing with integer ops), lets attributes be stored in-line with the object, and acts as a fast validity token—since maps form a persistent tree structure and change whenever an attribute is added, a pointer-identity check can confirm the cached layout is still current. An inline cache exploits this by caching a map/index pair per call site: on a map match it does a direct indexed load, otherwise it falls back to a string lookup and updates the cache; the fast path should be inlined and the slow path outlined. Built on CF Bolz-Tereick's "A Simple Object Model" sketch in roughly a page of Python code, this gives an accessible, self-contained implementation of instance attributes, maps, and interpreted inline caches, though real runtimes typically pair such caches with JIT compilers that generate native code rather than relying on the interpreted IC.

item.title: 20. Rule 30: one black cell
item.description:
11 points by amichail on 2026-10-22T22:16:48

Rule 30 is a one-dimensional cellular automaton defined by a single eight-entry rule (binary 00011110) that decides each new square from the three squares above it; starting from one black cell, it produces a pattern with a regular striped left side, a never-settling right side, and a centre column that passes standard randomness tests. This behaviour — simple rules yielding apparent randomness — was foundational to Stephen Wolfram's A New Kind of Science (2002), Rule 30 generated Mathematica's random integers, and its pattern adorns Cambridge North railway station. In October 2019 Wolfram offered three $10,000 prizes for questions about the centre column, read as a coin flip: whether it is always non-periodic, whether black and white occur equally often on average, and whether computing its nth cell requires at least n steps; seven years on, all three remain open, since a billion computed cells look random but prove nothing. The page reports two exact structural findings (dated 9 October 2026): on the left, diagonals eventually settle into eternal stripes, giving an exact boundary — starting near the apex and leaning outward at about 0.244 squares per row (close to, but not proven equal to, the ~0.246 speed at which changes spread leftward) — while on the right, white triangles touching the edge arrive at perfectly regular intervals, their widths set by the highest power of 2 dividing the row number, because each diagonal repeats with a power-of-2 period; neither order reaches the deep centre column, where diagonal periods run into the millions. Further explorations show that if the centre column repeated, the adjacent column would fall onto a 56-step wheel (equivalent to 8- and 7-step clocks) driven by perturbations from further right, and that a repeating centre would force the entire left side to eventually turn permanently white — a counterexample to Problem 1. Conversely, any desired sequence (primes, π in binary, a name) can be built into the centre from an infinite start constructed one square leftward at a time, but a finite start of n squares buys only about one correct step, and flipping one bit of the start changes the picture only inside a cone whose right edge advances exactly one square per step and whose left edge advances about a quarter square per step through the random region, reaching the centre after as many steps as its distance in squares.

item.title: 22. Hedra is a 3D open world game I wrote from scratch while in highschool
item.description:
181 points by maxilevi on 2026-10-22T18:44:36

Project Hedra is an open-source, low-poly open-world RPG built on a custom game engine the author began in high school (~15 years old) as an OpenGL learning exercise; it now spans roughly 100k lines of C# with first-class Linux and Windows support. Gameplay features procedurally generated worlds (voxel-based, meshed via Marching Cubes, with no world save file — only the seed and player data persist), quests and bosses, 100+ items with rarities, a skill tree, four classes with two specializations each, procedurally placed structures, fishing, crafting, trading, NPCs, companions and pets, multiple dimensions, navigation, and a soundtrack. The engine includes a modern OpenGL renderer with skinned mesh rendering, screen-space reflections and ambient occlusion, bloom/FXAA/MSAA, shadows, frustum and occlusion culling, LOD mesh simplification, a particle system, Bullet physics integration, an infinite chunk system, a data-oriented entity component system, custom low-GC primitives and allocators, over 1000 test cases with mocking/integration frameworks, OpenAL sound, Python (IronPython) modding support, Steam integration, CI-driven beta deploys, localization, and a raw-OpenGL UI toolkit — with the game architecturally structured as a mod atop the engine to keep the mod API maintained. The name "Hedra" derives from tetrahedra, the shape used in the original Marching Tetrahedra isosurface extraction; models are loaded as untextured plaintext .PLY and .DAE files, and a formerly multiplayer P2P/UDP hole-punching server remains as an artifact in the codebase.

item.title: 26. Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
item.description:
216 points by molind on 2026-10-22T09:31:18

earstrip is a polygon triangulator published as a single C++ header plus a WebAssembly build on npm under the ISC license (the same license as earcut), taking the same arguments as earcut; it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp in C++ and 1.4–2.1× faster than earcut.js in the browser, and the post explains how that was achieved. Because GPUs only fill triangles, every map polygon must be triangulated before rendering, and the engine's previous constrained Delaunay triangulator took 2.93 seconds on one M4 Pro core for the 3,740,425 polygons in an offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship — although Delaunay guarantees well-shaped triangles, flat fills don't need them, and nearly half the polygons have four vertices or fewer. Replacing it with ear clipping — cutting off "ears" (convex corners with nothing reaching into them) until n vertices become n − 2 triangles, guaranteed to exist by Meisters' 1975 theorem — was rebuilt idea by idea, with each commit timed on the same 3.7 million polygons: a naive version took 1,119 ms (2.6× faster than Delaunay but quadratic and slower than Delaunay on the 1,123 largest polygons); restricting ear tests to reflex "dent" vertices, which are the only ones that can block an ear, dropped it to 882 ms; skipping tests on convex polygons (detected via dent count plus exactly two x-direction changes, which correctly rejects self-winding stars) gave 880 ms; and emitting convex rings as zig-zag triangle strips, extending strips by cutting neighbour ears alternately, reached 762 ms. Holes, present in 11,345 polygons, are handled by cutting them open and stitching each to the outer ring with a bridge found via Eberly's rightmost-vertex ray method, choosing the first edge whose far endpoint is not obscured — with special cases for grid-aligned rays passing through vertices and holes touching the boundary at a single point.

item.title: 28. Jailbreaking the Switch 2
item.description:
774 points by ledoge on 2026-10-22T08:01:52

ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Nintendo Switch 2 on firmware 23.0.1, reportedly the first of its kind, allowing arbitrary native code execution as any ordinary sysmodule or the built-in fs sysmodule — enabling homebrew, game modding, save backup, and MMIO peripheral access. The exploit chain begins with userspace code execution via a 32-bit integer overflow in SmileBASIC's BASIC interpreter (the REMOVE command wraps position + count, letting an out-of-bounds memmove pull the array's own pointer into its length field for arbitrary read/write), rather than via WebKit, which is blocked by XOM, PAC, and CFI mitigations. From there, a buffer overflow in fs's GetEntryType path normalization (a fixed 0x0301-byte heap buffer receives an unbounded path) is exploited against a BufferedStorage cache entry to gain arbitrary read/write in the fs sysmodule, after which the process's saved PID is set to 1 to obtain FullPermission and dump internal storage and sysmodule code. Arbitrary r/w in fs is then converted to native code execution by swapping the ExeFS object behind the loader's IPC handle with a custom filesystem serving the original valid main.npdm but an arbitrary main executable — the signature chain still validates because fs submits the genuine NCA header hash beforehand — with timing controlled by replacing the event handle fs waits on. Finally, launching code under the ro sysmodule's NPDM grants kernel SVCs (SetProcessMemoryPermission, MapProcessCodeMemory, MapProcessMemory), and a KProcess handle to fs is obtained by overwriting an IEventNotifier handle with 0xffff8001. The author notes roughly two weeks of substantial work on the jailbreak itself, done with assistance from Codex agents running on a harness of JetKVMs and a Bluetooth-controlled power-button actuator; a Codex-modded Mario Kart World was created separately in a day as a demonstration, not via the "make no mistakes" jailbreak prompt shown in the setup photo.

item.title: 32. MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada
item.description:
246 points by Teever on 2026-10-22T14:26:40

A CBC News analysis conducted with the University of Bristol found that viewers of seven televised 2026 NHL playoff games featuring Canadian teams were exposed to about 3,000 gambling messages — two to three per minute via rink boards, jerseys, helmets, logos and commercial breaks — with 95% carrying no harm-reduction or age-restriction information, little changed since a similar 2024 study. The findings come as problem gambling and gambling-related suicides rise in Ontario following the province's 2022 legalization of private online casinos and sports betting, and as a recovering 22-year-old gambler describes the ads as triggering relapses. Federal Bill S-211, sponsored by MP Bardish Chagger and Senator Marty Deacon and already passed by the Senate, will be voted on by the standing committee on Canadian heritage in late October; it would require the federal government to acknowledge online gambling harms and consult on stricter rules, with Chagger hoping for eventual bans on sportswear and live-event gambling promotions, restricted hours, and prohibitions on celebrity endorsements. Ontario and Alberta oppose the bill as a two-tier system threatening provincial revenue, while a dozen mental health organizations and 28 addictions researchers back national action and the Canadian Gaming Association argues provinces should set their own standards. Researchers note countries such as Belgium, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany impose stricter limits, including near-total sports sponsorship bans and 9 p.m. advertising curfews.

Combining high-resolution coronary CT angiography and cardiometabolic profiling with CaRi-Heart and CaRi-Plaque® analysis, the study found coronary inflammation in 42.9% of participants — 17.9% with very high inflammation in at least one major artery — frequently occurring despite no plaque buildup or blockage; about 47% of those with no detectable plaque still showed elevated perivascular inflammation. item.title: 36. Show HN: agent-usage-guard – a Claude Code mod to protect your usage window
item.description:
23 points by zzyyxx332211 on 2026-10-22T18:02:38

agent-usage-guard is a Claude Code mod (~2,400 lines of TypeScript, no dependencies) that prevents runaway token spend before it happens, addressing cases where a single research prompt spawned 394 subagent calls (341 concurrent) and burned 84M context tokens in ten minutes, locking the user out until the usage window reset. Running inside Claude Code v2.1.287+, it reads the plan's live 5-hour and weekly usage percentages and gates agents, prompts, and tool calls against configurable rules: plan-window thresholds (asks at 80%, refuses at 95%), machine-wide agent caps (4 concurrent, 12 starts and 10M subagent tokens per 10 minutes, depth 1), context limits (notes at 300k, asks at 500k, tool-call throttles at 400k, idle-cache-expiry asks at 150k tokens with 1 hour idle), and loop protection (refuses 3 identical consecutive tool failures, pauses spawns after 5 refusals in 10 minutes). When the user is present it asks via Claude Code's own question dialog, and an approval lifts that condition until it clears or times out; in headless modes (claude -p, Agent SDK, dontAsk) it refuses instead, with escalating messages telling Claude to stop, batch, or wait. It is local and privacy-minimal (no network, no processes; stores only counts, coarse context buckets, and 13-character tool fingerprints — never prompt text, tool inputs, or output), fails open if a hook errors (except an unjudgeable agent, which is refused), and does not block background notifications, other sessions' messages, or prompts after a usage limit. It complements Claude Code's native caps (20 concurrent subagents, three nesting levels) and idle compaction, covering paths those miss. Commands include /agent-guard status, allow, pause, resume, report, and help; settings are controlled via environment variables like AGENT_GUARD, AGENT_GUARD_WINDOW_SECONDS, and AGENT_GUARD_JOURNAL. The /agent-guard report logs lockouts, threshold crossings, wind-down notes, and every question/refusal by rule for up to 90 days.

Lockouts still went up, because lots of parallel main sessions use up the window too. item.title: 39. Crystal 1.22
item.description:
173 points by ksec on 2026-10-22T13:20:13

Crystal 1.22.0 is released with 251 changes from 33 contributors, available via GitHub Releases and official distribution channels. Key language and compiler changes: processes now exit immediately on EPIPE when writing to STDOUT/STDERR (opt out with `STDOUT.exit_on_broken_pipe = false`), constants can carry type declarations, `Process.fork` is removed after long deprecation, new macros add compile-time text operations (`StringLiteral#bytesize`, `NumberLiteral#chr`, `RangeLiteral#each` for chars) and constants `Crystal::ALL_FLAGS`/`USER_FLAGS` expose compile-time flags. The aarch64-linux-gnu and aarch64-linux-musl targets are promoted to Tier 1, and the first `aarch64-windows-msvc` builds ship. DWARF parsing was revamped for speed and lower memory use—on-demand section scanning, an indexed table, LRU-cached backtrace lines, and DWARF 5 support. HTTP gained many fixes and improvements, including moving `#remote_address`/`#local_address` to `HTTP::Context`, adding `HTTP::Headers#merge`, and stricter validation (some breaking changes to `#body=`/`#content_length=` return values). All targets now use a native event loop based on the system selector by default (epoll on Solaris, kqueue on remaining BSDs), with libevent becoming opt-in and slated for deprecation; Kernel TLS support was enabled by default but reverted in 1.22.1. Other additions include `follow_symlinks:` args for `File.exists?` and `File::Info` predicates, `Char::Reader.new(Bytes)`, `Time::Span#to_nanoseconds`, `GC.syscall`, `LLVM::Type#size`/`#alignment`, LLVM 23.1/24.0 support, and static-pie musl backtrace fixes. Uppercase instance/class variables are deprecated. RFC 30 sets forward compatibility: building Crystal 1.22 requires a stage-0 compiler at 1.14 or later.

item.title: 40. Amazon identifies Oct 17 PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure
item.description:
263 points by cubefox on 2026-10-22T11:50:36

Amazon Threat Intelligence detected exploitation of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) on Oct. 17, 2026, four days before the Oct. 21, 1400 UTC embargo lift, with an attempt against a MadPot honeypot from an anonymized IP — suggesting a threat actor had early access to exploit details, though how remains unclear. After disclosure, proof-of-concept exploits appeared hours earlier than the release, and multiple actors exploited the flaws from additional anonymized infrastructure, with varied payloads indicating distinct operators; broad exploitation is now underway, and it is unconfirmed whether the attempts would have succeeded against real systems. Key lessons: an embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug, so public disclosure is not the earliest date of exploitation and investigations should start from Oct. 17; and AI-assisted analysis has cut the patch-to-exploit time so drastically that patch SLAs for critical internet-facing flaws should be measured in hours, not days, and defenses should not depend on CVE-specific signatures. AWS's internal threat intelligence detected and blocked the scanning, analyzing over 200 billion events per minute and drawing on its MadPot honeypot network. Recommended actions: upgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions (the only complete remediation, with no configuration-only workaround), consider blocking multi-part file uploads where patching is delayed after assessing application impact, watch for POST requests containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, and review web server logs for suspicious activity or unexpected process execution or file modification. Listed IOCs are six IP addresses (103.216.220.92 observed 10/17; 31.223.184.166, 37.19.200.5, 134.209.159.64, 103.114.163.188, and 95.217.98.37 on 10/21) that belong to shared anonymization infrastructure and should be investigated rather than blocked outright.

item.title: 41. OpenAI CLI
item.description:
235 points by armcat on 2026-10-22T05:23:11

The OpenAI CLI (`openai`) lets you call the OpenAI REST API directly from a terminal or shell script—generating images, uploading and downloading files, submitting batch jobs, exporting data as JSON/JSONL for piping to tools like `jq`, and querying admin endpoints—without writing an application; it's distinguished from Codex CLI (`codex`), which is a coding agent for working on projects. Installation is via prebuilt binaries from GitHub Releases, Homebrew (`brew install openai/tools/openai`), or Go (`go install github.com/openai/openai-cli/cmd/openai@latest`, requiring Go 1.26+), with authentication through `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY`. Commands follow the API's resource structure (`openai [flags]`), support help without a network connection, offer output formats (text by default, plus `json`, `jsonl`, `raw`, `yaml`), GJSON-based `--transform` field extraction, and `--format-error` for API error details; JSON input can be read from files via `@path`, with `OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN=1` guarding against untrusted piped input. The CLI also provides shell completion, an image picker (`Ctrl+X`, Tab), update checks that can be disabled with `OPENAI_CLI_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`, and documentation covering images, files, batches, audio, tokenization, webhooks, and output formats. The project is Apache 2.0 licensed and accepts bug reports via GitHub issues, with pull requests limited to collaborators; an official Terraform provider is noted for managing OpenAI resources as code.

Several Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative vulnerability reports were posted to the public Linux kernel mailing list instead of the private security list, apparently by mistake, prompting Linux maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question each submission. The disclosed issues include two CVSS 9.0 flaws — an SMB Direct remote code execution bug from an integer underflow (ZDI-CAN-33549), for which a patch exists in a branch intended for Linux v7.5, and a KSMBD race condition enabling remote code execution (ZDI-CAN-33774) — plus an skbuff skb_zerocopy local privilege escalation (ZDI-CAN-33367, already reported separately with a patch pending), an out-of-bounds write in the VMWGFX VMware graphics driver (ZDI-CAN-34068), an uninitialized resource in NVMeT code exposing information (ZDI-CAN-34076), and a search-domain TCP query stack buffer overflow allowing local privilege escalation (ZDI-CAN-32005). None are patched in mainline yet, though some fixes are in testing or queued in "-next" branches, and the flow of such reports continues amid growing AI-related bug discovery.

item.title: 43. Most Americans Say AI Is Bad for Society, Oppose More Data Centers
item.description:
81 points by karakoram on 2026-10-22T20:51:23

An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll of 2,545 U.S. adults (Oct. 9–13, 2026, ±2 points) finds that 57% of Americans say AI is bad for society versus 42% who say it's good, with negative views strongest among those under 30 (65%), Democrats (63%) and independents (58%), while Republicans split 51% good to 47% bad. People are slightly more positive about AI personally (50% good, 49% bad), though pessimism is more intense. Majorities see high risks: hacking of secure systems (73%), job elimination (65%), losing the ability to decide things without AI (62%), rising economic inequality (54%), and 33% see a high risk of human extinction. Far fewer see major benefits — 34% say AI has a big chance of making everyday tasks easier, 30% of U.S. AI dominance, 20% of greater productivity, and just 13% of creating many new jobs. Two-thirds say the federal government isn't regulating AI enough, and two-thirds disapprove of Trump's handling of it (80% approval among MAGA Republicans, but only 49% among non-MAGA Republicans); about half trust neither party on AI, though Democrats edge Republicans 26% to 19%. Two-thirds oppose building new data centers nationally, rising to 72% if one were built in their own community, with opposition cutting across party lines (81% of Democrats, 76% of independents, 58% of Republicans), age and geography, though 53% of MAGA Republicans support them.

item.title: 45. UN says breaching 1.5C warming limit is 'imminent and unavoidable'
item.description:
38 points by dabinat on 2026-10-22T23:37:50

A UN Environment Programme Emissions Gap report finds the globe will imminently and unavoidably exceed the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree Celsius warming target, reframing the goal as limiting the "overshoot" — the lowest-impact pathway would peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C and return to 1.5 C by 2100, requiring emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 from 2025 levels, a tripling of renewable electricity capacity by 2035, coal phaseout by 2040, and large-scale carbon removal. Existing pledges fall far short, yielding only 5-to-8% cuts by 2030 and implying a 2.6-degree peak, while current policies point to about 2.8 degrees — a figure that rose partly due to the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement — and even full achievement of all commitments peaks at 2.1 degrees. The report warns that every five years of emissions at current levels adds roughly 0.1 C, and scientists cited note each fraction of a degree raises risks of irreversible ice sheet, permafrost, ocean circulation and coral damage while costing over $1.2 trillion in annual GDP and exposing some 140 million more people to dangerous heat, though experts add that overshooting 1.5 C signals insufficient progress rather than doom, with the real task being rapid cuts in greenhouse gas tons.

item.title: 48. Show HN: Replacing CAPTCHAs with adaptive proof-of-work in WordPress
item.description:
11 points by MatthiasNordwig on 2026-10-22T13:03:14

This is a WordPress anti-spam plugin that blocks spam invisibly using a proof-of-work challenge solved by the visitor's browser in a few milliseconds — no CAPTCHAs, checkboxes, puzzles, or any user interaction. Rather than shipping integrations for specific form builders, it identifies submissions by their request signature, so it covers WordPress logins, registrations and comments, WooCommerce checkout and reviews, dozens of popular form plugins (Contact Form 7, WPForms, Elementor Pro Forms, Gravity Forms, Fluent Forms, and many more) pre-configured out of the box, plus any custom or unrecognized form trained in under a minute via a direct analysis mode. It runs entirely on the user's own server with no accounts, API keys, third-party scripts, cookies, or visitor data leaving the site, keeping privacy compliance and Core Web Vitals intact while imposing real compute costs on mass-spam bots. Features include adaptive difficulty during spam waves, per-site handling options (block, flag, or collect in a spam inbox), login brute-force protection with optional Fail2Ban support, and a lightweight footprint of a few kilobytes of JavaScript; the only stated limitation is that externally hosted forms (Typeform, Jotform, HubSpot, etc.) submit data outside WordPress and therefore cannot be checked. The changelog through version 6.2.0 lists numerous detection additions, fixes to WooCommerce cart and checkout handling, and security improvements such as no longer storing card numbers, CVCs, IBANs, or password fields.

item.title: 49. Show HN: CATT 0.2.1: Test agents/services against a Muse/Instinct-alike, in CI
item.description:
7 points by botacode on 2026-10-22T22:18:40

Consumer Agent Testing Tool (CATT) is an open-source (MIT) test harness that runs scripted or model-driven agents against an MCP server, MCP app, website, or HTTP API to verify what the service actually did, inspect evidence, and diff results across builds. It supports Muse (default) and Instinct as surrogate emulation targets using a shared connector testing contract covering routing, memory, payments, browser/HTTP tasks, and scheduling, though CATT is explicitly a surrogate test host rather than a certification of compatibility with any real assistant, and each Muse-specific behavior carries a recorded basis (documented, unofficial, assumed, or unknown). Its lanes include connector runs (tool use, account/approval rules, private values, outcome checks), connector extensions, scenario scaffolding, readiness/guideline checks for Muse and Instinct, Personal Agent Protocol and gadget registration checks, MCP protocol conformance, embedded MCP app runs in Chromium, website browsing with takeover pause, HTTP API runs with per-call approval binding, and evidence report/export/replay/diff. Setup requires Python 3.12+, uv, and Node.js 20+ (plus Chromium for app/browser lanes), with a `doctor` command to verify the environment; scripted runs need no model account, while agent runs need a model profile and API key. The docs provide quickstarts for the connector lane (a loopback Cedar Stays-style fixture with no account), popular MCP servers, and a hosted Coverage Cat sandbox, plus notes that three features relying on macOS Seatbelt are unsupported on Linux.

item.title: 1. There isn't an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability
item.description:
480 points by zkldi on 2026-10-21T23:13:27

A newly disclosed PHP vulnerability is real and deserves patching, but it is being wildly overhyped: despite thousands of purported PoC exploits circulating on GitHub within hours of disclosure, none work against a vanilla PHP instance. Unlike trivially weaponizable past catastrophes such as Log4Shell, Heartbleed, Shellshock, or Rails YAML deserialization — which botnets exploited almost immediately — no working exploit exists for this bug, even with tens of thousands of people and LLMs attempting one. Many of the fake PoCs are produced with AI assistance and quietly rely on the target already having a severe local-file-inclusion flaw, or they even modify the test server to insert a vulnerability, making the "proof" meaningless. The author argues this reveals a troubling pattern: people outsource security judgment to LLMs, producing bizarre, uniform reasoning errors ("decision Schelling points") — such as adding a vulnerability to a server to demonstrate the server is vulnerable. Panic was fueled by a PHP core team member's apocalyptic warning, PHP's reputation for insecurity, and anxiety about the LLM era. The conclusion: this is not a Log4J-level event and is far harder to exploit than claimed, though servers should still be patched.

On October 21, 2026, GitLab released versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13 for CE/EE, containing bug and security fixes, and urges all self-managed installations to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com is already patched, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0 or 19.4.2-internal0 or later need no action. The most severe fix is CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS 10.0), an integer overflow in the regular expression compiler that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution via a crafted regex; the fix was backported to older versions and GitLab released two threat detections for exploitation attempts. Other fixes include CVE-2026-15723 (CVSS 8.2), an OmniAuth-to-LDAP auto-linking flaw enabling account takeover; CVE-2026-112212 (7.5), cache poisoning of OAuth/OIDC discovery endpoints that could redirect flows to attacker-controlled servers; CVE-2026-12664 (6.8), a GraphQL work item email field scope bypass; CVE-2026-16255 (5.9), incomplete enforcement of SAML/LDAP membership locks in EE; plus lower-severity issues involving leaked internal server credentials, unauthorized milestone metadata reads from private projects via the group milestones API, unauthorized access to paid AI features, exposure of confidential issue titles through merge request title caching, bypass of merge request approval policies, permanent deletion of vulnerability records by read-only users, and re-enabling Amazon Q data egress despite a Duo admin lock. Most vulnerabilities were reported through HackerOne, with a few found internally; details become public on the issue tracker 90 days after patching. The patch includes database migrations — causing downtime on single-node instances but not with proper zero-downtime procedures on multi-node setups — and GitLab recommends always running the latest patch for your supported version.

item.title: 3. Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI Installs a Credential Stealer and Backdoor
item.description:
494 points by abhisek on 2026-10-21T14:00:26

LiteLLM 1.107.0, published to PyPI and Docker on 2026-10-21, contained a credential stealer and remote code execution backdoor that were absent from the upstream GitHub source. Installing it drops three files into site-packages — cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py — which execute in every Python process on the host, even ones that never import litellm. The cook.py stealer collects SSH keys, cloud and CI/CD credentials, browser passwords, shell history, AI tool tokens, GPG/TLS keys, and LLM provider keys from a LiteLLM proxy database, encrypts them (AES-256-CBC with an RSA-OAEP-wrapped key), and POSTs them to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck once per host. sitecustomize.py forks a detached hourly daemon that reads a server address from an attacker-controlled GitHub file, reruns the stealer, and executes whatever code it downloads as "codepy". The implant entered via one extra line in the sdist's pyproject.toml (maturin's `data = "cook"`) that copies the malicious folder into the wheel. Per LiteLLM's incident report, the attacker stole GitHub CLI credentials of three developers from an exposed internal deployment, bypassed branch protection using an owner's token to point the release workflow at a lookalike repository (Berri-AI/litellm), passed the approval gate with a second credential, and had the official pipeline build and sign the artifacts. PyPI removed the release by 13:23 UTC and Docker tags by 14:20 UTC; the attacker's GitHub account disappeared around 13:40 UTC, disabling the backdoor loop, though hosts infected earlier may have run second-stage code. Versions 1.106.2, 1.107.0rc1, 1.107.0rc2, and the pinned companion packages are clean. Indicators of compromise include the three planted files, /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb, /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock, the PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE=1 variable, the X-Token upload header, and specific SHA-256 hashes and image digests published with the advisory.

item.title: 4. Using LLM for confidence scoring is a bad idea
item.description:
69 points by jimauthors on 2026-10-21T04:27:51

LLM-generated confidence scores cannot be trusted because an autoregressive model simply writes a plausible number as the next token rather than measuring anything; the score changes with rephrasing or repeat asks, reflects the preceding text rather than the evidence, and is never calibrated against actual accuracy—only against predicting the next token during pretraining. A genuine confidence score must (1) reflect how much information the prediction rests on and (2) be verified against outcomes on the same kind of question, which requires keeping a record of predictions and results (as with a weather forecaster whose stated probabilities match observed rates). Instead, agent designers should build an external calibration rule: choose observable features of each task (e.g., whether a help-center article was found, whether repeated runs agree), start from the historical base rate, log every prediction and outcome, update the rule so each feature group's confidence equals its observed success rate, and recheck periodically for over- or under-confidence. Such a rule is deterministic for a given set of inputs, independent of wording, calibrated on one's own data, and improves with every recorded case—though it is only as good as the record kept.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. I looked at how consistent LLMs are by asking them to forecast events from Polymarket with slight variations in the input, such as negating the question.You can see for yourself the results here: https://noisebench.com/
  2. I got a degree in statistics, and what I remember from those times is that we spent maybe 10% of our time learning how to build the model and 90% of the time correctly interpreting the model output. Of course, in the time I learned statistics it was almost exclusively applied in hard science, finance, and actuary. The wild west of machine learning hadn't gotten started. I wonder if they teach it differently now.When we start using big datasets where n went into the tens of millions we kinda stopped bothering because margins were so small it was effectively certain you found the mean of some range. However I think in that time we forget what confidence scoring actually is and how quickly multiplied alpha can balloon on you.
  3. Of course an LLM does have a latent concept of its own confidence that is not useless, and is perfectly able to articulate it, the author just chose the worst possible way to ask. Using a 0-100 scale for anything is a bad idea with both LLMs and people. Instead of rating it 0-100, split your problem into many dimensions/axes and give each a small and meaningful enum or just a less granular numerical scale (ideally just a binary choice). Then apply weighted scoring to the result. You'll be surprised how much better it becomes at meaningfully expressing its confidence this way.YouTube removed the 1-5 scale for the same reason, people have no idea what to do with it.

item.title: 6. Rust Style Guide
item.description:
284 points by kaycebasques on 2026-10-21T19:11:57

Google's Rust style guide governs Rust usage across google3, Android, ChromeOS, Fuchsia, and Chrome, covering not just formatting but API and implementation design to keep code consistent and maintainable. Its goals prioritize readability and maintainability over ease of writing, favor rules that support automation and Large-Scale Changes (LSCs), align with the wider Rust ecosystem where possible, include only rules with tangible benefit, and minimize bikeshedding. Official public Rust style rules apply except where they conflict with this guide; deviations exist mainly to make code easier for tooling to refactor. API design rules are binding for library code but only strongly recommended for application code, which should favor simplicity over reusability. On code organization, Chromium prefers small, focused crates (ideally single-file) and a flat file layout within each crate, names source files and leaf modules after their primary item, keeps implementation code out of non-leaf modules, and discourages glob imports (with narrow exceptions such as merging C++ namespaces privately) since they complicate LSCs. Import conventions: each `use` statement pulls from one module; traits are usually imported locally within functions; top-level functions are called qualified with their module name while types and traits are imported and used unqualified (with exceptions for ambiguity, large type groups, macros, and heavy-dependency code). Formatting should use the appropriate tool (e.g., `git cl format`), with configured rustfmt options including 100-column lines, lowercase hex literals, macro matcher formatting, and escapes for invisible characters; codebases may skip options unavailable on stable Rust, and automatic formatting can be opted out of where needed.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Apply #[non_exhaustive] to publicly-exposed enums seems like a crazy recommendation to me. So much of the power of enums is that when you add a new case the compiler will flag all pattern matches that you need to update, which is a good thing because you're forced to consider each case. Having a catch-all saves dev-time but it risks not appropriately handling new cases becoming a runtime issue instead of a compile time error.
  2. Can anyone expand on the chromium specifc guidelines on super tiny crates, particularly no nesting of modules/source files?That feels like the ~2010 era of people saying that functions should be as small as possible. That lead me to reviewing a lot of code where every function was one or two lines and you couldn't actually see what was going on anymore through the layers of unneeded abstraction.I want to give chrome the benefit of the doubt, but that seems really goofy.
  3. > Type names should be imported and used unqualifiedThis just pushes people to have redundant information in types (`IoError` instead of `io::Error`).Unless a type is widely recognized (like `HashMap`), I prefer to have them fully qualified so I have the contextual meaning for it. If I am working with a generic name like `Source`, what does that mean? I shouldn't have to look up in the imports to understand the code (or only understand it through an LSP).Reducing imports also reduces unnecessary merge conflicts.

item.title: 8. mitmproxy adds --emudhra option
item.description:
426 points by ahlCVA on 2026-10-21T23:51:37

This code diff widens private-key type hints across a TLS certificate store module so that functions and data structures (`dummy_cert`, `dummy_crl`, `CertStoreEntry`, `CertStore`, `load_pem_private_key`) accept either `rsa.RSAPrivateKey` or `ec.EllipticCurvePrivateKey` instead of RSA keys only. It also adds a new constant, `EMUDHRA_CHAIN_PEM`, containing a private key plus certificate chain for a compromised eMudhra intermediate CA ("EM OV TLS CA - G3C") and its cross-signed root ("emSign Root TLS CA - G3"), with a comment pointing to https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ for details. The change is embedded near existing DH parameter data in the certificate handling code.

item.title: 10. Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
item.description:
70 points by kmansm27 on 2026-10-21T16:44:53

Omnara is an open-source (Apache 2.0) managed agent platform — a self-hostable alternative to Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API — for running AI agents on any model and any machine with tools, secrets, permissions, and streaming built in. Agents are configured via a simple `agent.yaml` file and launched through a CLI (Node.js 22+), a TypeScript SDK (`@omnara/sdk`), or a REST API, and can be chatted with in the terminal or monitored in a dashboard. Its architecture consists of an API, Postgres (which stores every agent step as durable state so workers can resume agents after crashes), stateless workers that run the agent loop, and machines running an outbound-connecting `omnarad` daemon so agents can execute commands on laptops, VMs, or containers without inbound ports or SSH keys. It supports any compatible model provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Bedrock, LiteLLM, Ollama, self-hosted), built-in tools plus MCP and custom tools, reusable skills, persistent memory stores, subagents, sandbox pools from eleven providers, cron schedules, Slack/Discord/GitHub integrations, event streaming and webhooks, per-tool approval permissions, RBAC and shared secrets, and multi-tenancy. It can be self-hosted free via Docker Compose (keeping agent history in your own Postgres) or used as Omnara Cloud, which is free with your own keys and machines. Compared with the hosted competitors, Omnara works with any model, runs anywhere, and keeps data queryable in your own database; it's positioned as the choice for those wanting model/machine flexibility or self-hosting, complementing workflow builders, agent frameworks, terminal harnesses, and hosted agent platforms. Example configurations include a Slack coding agent, a PR review agent, an SRE agent, and a browser agent.

item.title: 11. Today's PHP security release, and how we're strengthening security
item.description:
723 points by ejohnso49 on 2026-10-21T15:48:56

PHP released versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, fixing two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) affecting memory management and error handling — core areas touched by nearly every request. The first stems from out-of-memory corruption, where hitting PHP's memory_limit at a critical moment left partially initialized data that was later treated as valid, enabling RCE on Apache with mod_php and confirmed exploits on PHP-FPM; the second is a stale global state use-after-free where a fatal error left state pointing to freed memory from a previous request. First signs of the OOM issue surfaced during a 2024 external audit by Quarkslab (funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency via OSTIF), but a fix stalled for months over trade-off debates and consensus-based decision-making — a failure the project attributes to process flaws and lack of resources. Since then PHP has reorganized its security work: a Foundation Ecosystem Security Team was created in May 2026, staff including Alexandre Daubois and Daniel Scherzer were hired, AI tools (Claude Mythos, OpenAI's Daybreak Red) were added for report validation, and audits by Calif (via the Patch the Planet program), OpenAI, Wiz, and Trail of Bits ultimately revealed the full exploitability of the OOM bug, making it the top priority from August 11. Coordinated disclosure was disrupted when CVE IDs leaked on October 20 with a wrong CVSS score, Calif accidentally published a proof-of-concept video, and Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo by releasing patched images over six hours early; the release was moved up by a day as a compromise. The project urges companies, hosting providers, governments, and public institutions that depend on PHP to sponsor the PHP Foundation, since security work rests on a small group of engineers and growing AI-found bug reports require experienced people to judge fixes and weigh compatibility trade-offs.

item.title: 12. DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS “Cinnamon Teal”
item.description:
403 points by nnx on 2026-10-21T14:01:22

DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS, codenamed "Cinnamon Teal," is the project's largest feature release to date, built from nearly 20,000 commits since 1.5. It is a long-term support release backed until at least October 2027; the previous LTS (1.4) remains supported until late November 2026, and 1.5 support has been extended to March 2027. Highlights include a polished Quack client-server protocol with a new CONNECT statement for attaching to remote databases (also usable with PostgreSQL and MySQL, with a remote pushdown optimizer) plus CLI `-serve`/`-connect` shortcuts; asynchronous I/O for Parquet, CSV, and native storage that dramatically speeds up remote reads on object storage; full integration of the VARIANT type for semi-structured data, which detects common structure, "shreds" it for compression and columnar execution, and supports Parquet reading/writing plus `variant_*` functions; an agent mode in the CLI that detects coding agents and emits compact Markdown, JSON errors, and query cost estimates (cutting output volume by 59% on TPC-H); a new PEG-based extensible parser as the default (replacing the 2018 YACC/Bison parser, revertible via `enable_legacy_parser`), letting extensions hook into the grammar; a revamped C API v2; trusted extension repositories that organizations can host and sign themselves; core extension updates including DuckLake 1.1, Iceberg REST catalog support, and Delta table creation with time travel; and SQL triggers (BEFORE/AFTER, row/statement-level, transition tables, DROP TRIGGER), usable for audit tables and incremental materialized view maintenance, with some combinations not yet supported. Client libraries like Go, R, and Java lag a few days behind the CLI and Python releases.

item.title: 13. Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover vulnerabilities
item.description:
251 points by nr378 on 2026-10-21T14:03:43

OpenAI led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical PHP vulnerabilities, one of which was identified using GPT-5.6 Sol under the "Patch the Planet" initiative (Wiz independently discovered and reported both flaws). PHP's maintainers led the fixes and release, with Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research and coordination; organizations using PHP should now apply the fixes, aided by a PHP version checker available as a Codex skill. Given PHP's widespread use, this is considered one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory, and it marks a case where frontier AI found vulnerabilities before attackers did—though the same capabilities could help attackers build exploits. OpenAI has committed $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access through Daybreak for Frontline Defenders for under-resourced organizations protecting essential services. The post proposes a five-stage framework for responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software: validate and fix the upstream flaw (with adversarial testing of patches); give affected organizations time to prepare mitigations, WAF rules, and older-release fixes; coordinate with government partners (including the White House's Super Intelligence Force, ONCD, CISA, and international agencies); prepare updates across affected products; then publish guidance and support deployment. Advance information is shared based on an organization's protective role, time needed, and ability to handle sensitive data, with timelines reassessed if exploitation or leaks occur. OpenAI also supports maintainers through funding, model access (Codex for OSS subscriptions, Rust Foundation sponsorship), and hands-on engineering help, while calibrating Daybreak blocking classifiers to limit misuse. Looking ahead, it highlights opportunities in secure-by-default coding, migration to memory-safe languages, formal verification, and stronger sandboxing, and it invites community feedback on disclosure windows, emergency patching, and early-notice practices.

item.title: 17. Postgres recovery_prefetch can cause outages
item.description:
20 points by plaur782 on 2026-10-21T22:33:08

PostgreSQL's `recovery_prefetch` feature — enabled by default since PostgreSQL 17 — can cause production outages, particularly in setups using synchronous replication. The problem was flagged as early as February 2021 during the feature's development, when Stephen Frost noted unnecessary prefetches of already-prefetched blocks were probably tolerable, and again in March 2025 when Michael Zhilin (Postgres Pro) reported replay lag of several hours on a standby, resolved by disabling `recovery_prefetch`; the prefetch code makes fadvise calls even when blocks are already loaded from WAL full-page images rather than disk. The deeper issue: when a primary does large sequential I/O, `recovery_prefetch` turns it into 8KB random reads on replicas, amplifying read IOPS by up to 16x and exhausting available IOPS (e.g., on 500-IOPS cloud disks). Combined with full-page writes (which most production installs enable for torn-write protection) and synchronous replication (increasingly common on Kubernetes/commodity hardware), this creates an outage: a burst of write activity plus a network glitch that interrupts WAL streaming sends the standby into WAL-restore mode, and because a standby won't resume streaming until it has caught up, all writes block for 30+ minutes or hours. This is trivially reproducible (a public repro repo is provided): run pgbench with synchronous replication, checkpoint and update ~5% of a table, then kill the walreceiver — TPS drops to zero. Disabling `recovery_prefetch` (while leaving full-page writes on) eliminates the read IOPS burst and lets the standby stay caught up. The author leans toward disabling `recovery_prefetch` broadly, doubting its value with full-page writes on by default, and also suggests running two standbys with quorum commit (ANY 1) to reduce the fragility of depending on a single WAL receiver connection.
