item.title: 19. Eight Bits of Trust: eMudhra's CA keys cracked in milliseconds
item.description:
882 points by hkc on 2026-10-21T09:08:08

Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities — six TLS CAs and two code-signing CAs, all created in April 2025 and cross-signed by Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root — had private keys that were trivially recoverable: each was a P-384 elliptic-curve key whose value was a single byte (the recovered values were 4, 56, 115, 155, 156, 230, 66, and 237), meaning anyone could brute-force all 256 possibilities in milliseconds from the public certificates. A researcher reported this on 17 October; Chrome blocked the intermediates via CRLSet that evening, Firefox via OneCRL hours later, and both moved to remove the eMudhra root entirely. Because the keys were effectively public from the moment the certificates existed, there is a 17-month exposure window with no way to know who else recovered them — which is why the compromise "cannot be contained." Certificate Transparency means no forged TLS certs reached Chrome by default, but non-browser clients (curl, Python, Node, Go, Java, package managers, CI/CD pipelines, server-to-server APIs, IoT/OT devices with frozen root stores, and Windows code-signing) typically trust on-disk CA bundles without checking revocation or CT, so revocation doesn't help them. The author verified that forged certificates for api.stripe.com were accepted by curl, Python, Node, and Windows CryptoAPI under default settings. The recommended fix is updating every CA bundle (OS ca-certificates, certifi, Node, Homebrew, container images); un-updatable devices will trust these CAs until the certificates expire in July 2039. eMudhra later attributed the incident to a ceremony script bug that generated a second weak key pair on the HSM, followed by human error selecting the wrong keys for the CSR — and the keys were also recoverable by a simple prompt to an AI agent.

item.title: 20. Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data
item.description:
142 points by raahelb on 2026-10-21T13:37:00

OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used thousands of AI agents powered by GPT-Rosalind to analyze a whole-brain CRISPR atlas—data on how gene disruptions affect millions of mouse brain cells—in just 32 minutes, a job estimated to take humans months to a year. Each agent studied one perturbation, cross-referenced scientific literature, and proposed mechanisms; their reports were merged into a publicly available "reasoning atlas" linking genes, cellular effects, publications, and possible mechanisms. Called distributed biological reasoning, the parallel approach outperformed a single agent given the whole dataset: at the largest workload the distributed agents cited over 700 references versus 11 for the single agent, and blinded human experts preferred the distributed reports 75% of the time and judged their novelty assessments as aligned with expert opinion. Notable findings include an unexpected divergence between Tsc1 and Tsc2—genes that both regulate mTOR—in the cerebellum, where Tsc2 disruption altered dozens of neuronal-communication genes while Tsc1 disruption had little effect, matching the TSC2-linked cerebellar abnormalities seen in tuberous sclerosis patients; and a lead involving DCTN1 (mutated in Perry syndrome), whose disruption raised cholesterol-production gene expression, suggesting altered neuronal cholesterol distribution might contribute to neurodegeneration. The aim is to help researchers extract more testable ideas from large biological experiments and prioritize follow-up work on disease mechanisms and treatments.

item.title: 22. Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability
item.description:
108 points by Maxious on 2026-10-21T14:11:14

Two PHP vulnerabilities disclosed by Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, tracked as php2shell — affect all servers running PHP 5.4 or later and can allow denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when specially crafted HTTP traffic is processed. The flaws stem from PHP mishandling memory when a request is interrupted: in one case an out-of-memory interruption leaves internal data uninitialized and then used during cleanup, and in the other a fatal error leaves references to memory freed when the request ends, so a later request in the same process follows stale references and may expose sensitive data. Because PHP runs on nearly 70% of websites and underpins platforms like WordPress and Magento, the impact could be broad; the flaws live in the PHP runtime itself, so updating the PHP interpreter (or asking a hosting provider to do so) is required — updating application code or plugins alone does not fix them. Cloudflare coordinated mitigation with the PHP Foundation, OpenAI and Wiz, deploying WAF protections about nine hours before public disclosure so that free and paid WAF customers were covered starting October 21, 3:02 UTC, and it observed attack traffic with payloads being mutated to bypass its rules even before the official release. Because request data alone often cannot distinguish exploits from legitimate traffic, Cloudflare built a new "full transaction detection" capability that correlates request and response signals within one HTTP transaction, allowing a matching origin response to be blocked before it reaches the requester; php2shell protections are the first managed detections released using it. New "Anomalous Execution" rules have shipped in the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba, seven rule IDs) for Free users with no action needed, and in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee) for Professional, Business and Enterprise plans, which should confirm block mode; a high-confidence signature rule (afffe22785674c80a31875c848d2242a) is also deployed to the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default on all plans including Free. Customers can review blocked events under Security > Security Analytics > Events, filter by the listed rule IDs, and narrow the Managed Ruleset scope as needed; Cloudflare advises patching PHP promptly while keeping WAF protections enabled as defense in depth, restricting uploads and limiting upload sizes to reduce exposure, and notes its analysts will keep updating rules as new techniques emerge, with changes trackable in the changelog.

item.title: 23. When Do We Become the Person We Ought to Be?
item.description:
30 points by toomuchtodo on 2026-10-21T23:57:41

A survey of 557 U.S. adults fielded in August 2025 (supported by a Notre Dame Sorin Fellows Program grant, with undergraduate Anna Bohlen) examines moral self-reflection and self-improvement by age and religiosity. Young adults (under 35) are far more likely than older ones to say they are "very" or "somewhat far" from being the kind of person they morally ought to be (38% vs. 6–14% among those 55+), while about half of the oldest group say they are "pretty close" or "already there." Older respondents are ~11 points more likely to report deliberately trying to improve their character daily, yet far less likely to rationally dwell on whether their actions were right or wrong — only a third of those 55+ reflect on their behavior most of the time or always. Practicing religious adults (attending at least monthly) reflect on morality much more than non-practicing or non-religious peers — e.g., 53% vs. 27% among the youngest — and among young adults the religious are also most likely to feel close to their moral ideal (34% vs. 19%), though this pattern reverses among those 55+, where nearly 6 in 10 non-religious elders feel they've "arrived" versus 47% of religious groups. A combined index (moral confidence minus reflection) shows young and middle-aged religious people in negative territory — reflecting heavily while feeling morally dissatisfied — while older non-religious retirees are the most positive, most content group. The author cautions that all measures are self-reported and subjective, since ideals of morality vary, possibly higher among religious traditions, concluding that self-improvement is essentially a young person's game and older adults are largely content with who they are. Ryan P. Burge is a professor of practice at the Danforth Center on Religion and Politics at Washington University.

item.title: 26. The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
item.description:
62 points by Klaster_1 on 2026-10-21T16:09:28

GitHub is migrating its Git repository storage from its own data centers to Azure, driven by surging agentic traffic, power capacity ceilings, and supply chain limits. Most repositories now have two of five replicas in Azure, with Azure serving roughly half of Git traffic; the migration sequence deliberately moved data first, then evolved the architecture. The remaining 0.00001% of repositories — the busiest — were blocked because Spokes' quorum waits for every healthy replica before proceeding, so a ~25ms cross-region round trip on each serialized write capped throughput. The fix narrows quorum serialization from whole repositories to individual references: since updates to different references (e.g., separate branches) are independent, they can proceed concurrently, and internal tests showed 3–4x higher throughput at lower latency. A second step, decoupling storage from compute, makes Azure Blob Storage a quorum member via an "ephemeral virtual replica" that streams writes to object storage (acknowledging only when durable) and coalesces disjoint-reference transactions into single I/O batches; this enables on-demand virtual read replicas that warm caches from blob storage without joining the quorum, so reads scale independently — in load tests they exceeded the harness's limits. Remaining challenges include in-line reconciliation for all read types and pushing write throughput further. The next phase, to be unveiled at GitHub Universe, targets write throughput by storing immutable Git objects without consensus and ordering only reference state, while retaining a small consensus group; Spokes' routing, API (100B+ ops/day), and background "sweeper" systems carry over.

A board game called Hitster uses QR-coded cards that map to songs played via Spotify or Apple Music, but its app requires a paid music subscription, prompting an effort to reverse engineer the Android APK and extract the card-to-track data. After decompiling the app with jadx, the author found a Base64-encoded, AES-GCM-encrypted JSON file in res/raw and located the full decryption routine in the code, which derives a 256-bit AES key by SHA-256-hashing the ciphertext length minus 28 concatenated with an unknown secret string. Finding that secret involved locating two 32-byte arrays in the code and XORing them together, yielding the string "XYPL63BjoWJJKCsxK69rH2NnuycMv3cY"; a Rust decryptor using this key then produced roughly 31,000 lines mapping card IDs to Spotify and Apple Music tracks and ISRCs across multiple regions (card IDs are region-specific). In the end, the whole exercise was unnecessary: the same data was freely downloadable, unencrypted, at a predictable URL on hitster.jumboplay.com/hitster-assets/gameset_database.json — roughly 18 hours of work to crack a non-secret.

item.title: 29. PHP web runtimes (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
item.description:
114 points by hayd on 2026-10-21T21:12:59

PHP2Shell is an AWS WAF (or WAF-style) rule that blocks requests matching a specific combination: the HTTP method must be exactly POST, the request must contain the string PHPSESSID either as a cookie key or anywhere in the body, and the body must also contain PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. When all three conditions are met, the request is blocked. The rule is named "PHP2Shell" with request sampling and CloudWatch metrics enabled under the metric name PHP2Shell, and all byte-match checks use no text transformations, with cookie and body fields set to continue on oversize content — targeting the PHP session upload progress race-condition technique used to turn file uploads into remote code execution.

item.title: 30. Your MCU likely escaped the eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
item.description:
60 points by hasheddan on 2026-10-21T16:05:05

The eMudhra Intermediate CA compromise (disclosed October 20, 2026) exposed eight intermediate CA private keys that were publicly accessible and trivially weak — one was literally the number 4 — letting anyone mint trusted leaf certificates for any trust store including eMudhra's root. Certificate Transparency logs show no misuse, so CT-enforcing browsers (Firefox, Chrome, Edge, Safari) were not attacked, but non-browser clients may have been; the disclosure triggered a rush of patches across languages, tools, OS packages, and TLS libraries to block the intermediates or the eMudhra root. While single-board computers and Linux-based IoT devices should be updated, MCU-class devices are largely safe: constrained by under-1MB storage and fixed firmware, they typically embed only the single root CA needed for a specific endpoint (e.g., the Zephyr HTTP sample ships just GlobalSign Root CA for google.com) rather than a full trust bundle, so unless the eMudhra or cross-signing Sectigo root was explicitly compiled in, they are not vulnerable. The author suggests the event is a chance to apply the intentionality of embedded design more broadly, while noting users still must patch CI environments, developer tooling, cloud services, and productivity software.

CleanFrame is a minimal, customizable home screen replacement for Samsung's The Frame TV, running on Tizen, that shows your apps, a photograph, and a simple 12-hour clock with a remote-friendly interface. It was built for one specific TV (Samsung QA55LS03DAWXXY / LS03D, firmware 2130.0, Tizen 9.0) and is shared as open source under the MIT licence with the caveat that it carries no compatibility guarantee — setup scripts, signing, and identities must be adapted and tested on your own hardware. A browser preview (Node.js 22+, Python 3.10+) lets you try and customize the interface first: choose List or Dock layout with icons/names, pick from fifteen wallpapers or a light/dark background, and adjust typography, focus, and pre-rendered glass/blur materials, with preferences saved locally. TV installation uses Samsung's Developer Mode, official tools, and your own certificates; installing the app and remapping the Home button are separate steps, and native Home/startup changes use undocumented helpers that can break after firmware updates, so a recovery baseline is recommended. Work with a local coding agent is encouraged, starting with bounded browser-only changes while preserving remote navigation and the ES5 runtime; source and Playwright checks (using isolated Chromium profiles, never contacting a TV) validate the build. The repo includes setup guides, device evidence and limits (e.g., unverified behavior after streaming/Art Mode), third-party notices for fonts and photos, and no affiliation with Samsung or streaming services. It works only on Tizen — Android TV, Google TV, webOS, and Roku would need separate implementations.

item.title: 33. Texas Continued Data Center Permitting After the Governor's Pause
item.description:
33 points by DeepLogin on 2026-10-21T19:03:23

On September 21, 2026, Governor Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt all permits sought by data centers and told no state agency to advance regulatory approvals for data centers until ERCOT, the Public Utility Commission, and the Texas Water Development Board complete reviews of their grid, water, and community impacts — a reversal of his earlier enthusiasm for data center growth in Texas, which is the nation's largest market for such development. TCEQ told FracTracker it had paused issuance of air and water permits and would not advance applications through review, but a review of TCEQ records conducted with Public Citizen found the agency kept moving data center projects forward after September 21: it mailed public-notice letters the day after the order for three major-source air permits (VoltaGrid, Nexus, and NRG Prairie projects), whose 30-day comment periods started while the public reasonably believed permitting had stopped; issued eleven construction stormwater authorizations, including for hyperscale sites like Caldwell Valley Technology Park, Crusoe's Abilene campus, and EdgeConneX's Cedar Creek campus, clearing them for grading and excavation; advanced 14 gas plant and generator applications through review, sometimes expediting them; and recorded seven emission-limit certifications as issued. The report also raises questions about how TCEQ defines infrastructure "directly supporting" data centers, citing stormwater approval for LCRA's $111.6 million Misty substation — linked to a developer's data center plans and a proposed 1,500 MW gas plant — and an expedited generator application for a 4,000-bed data center construction workforce camp, neither of which is labeled a data center project. Noting that identifying data center permits is difficult because applicants are often obscure LLCs or power companies, FracTracker calls for a centralized public data center permit tracker like Pennsylvania's, a statewide moratorium to allow cumulative-impact studies and community input, full TCEQ compliance with the pause, reopening of affected comment periods, and public disclosure of TCEQ's compliance update to the Governor.

It is simply because the tip of a quill and the nib of a traditional[1] fountain pen cannot move in any direction. The way you hold it if you are right handed forbids moving in the "backslash"* direction[2] upwards. You can "draw" from top down but not "shove" upwards in that direction. Since in joined script we start letters mostly from the baseline (and have connecting strokes) this makes the "right leaning slant" much easier to write.The anatomy of a right handed writer also plays a role. When you write fast, the hand pivots at the wrist and fingers as it moves rightward, and that produces a forward slant.[1] Modern fountain pen nibs have a little ball at tip. So even if you used on in primary school you might not have noticed the directional effect.[2] That is why the slash (virgula) has existed for centuries while the backslash is an invention of the computer age.

item.title: 35. Show HN: Sumi.css – CSS Framework
item.description:
86 points by bepero on 2026-10-21T12:50:33

Sumi.css is a minimalist, classless-first CSS framework that styles plain semantic HTML — headings, forms, tables, cards, accordions, modals and navigation — with no JavaScript, no dependencies and no build step. It ships as a single 6.7 KB minified/gzipped file (sumi.min.css), available via download or jsDelivr CDN, with a commented source file (sumi.css) for development. It supports light and dark mode automatically via system preference, with `data-theme` to force either mode anywhere on the page, and is fully themed through `--s-*` CSS custom properties covering colors, fonts, spacing, radii and shadows. Element styles are wrapped in `:where()` for zero specificity, so user CSS always overrides them without `!important`. Accessibility features include visible focus rings, ARIA-driven states (`aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, `aria-current`) and reduced-motion support. Optional utility classes and attributes extend behavior: `.container`, `.grid` with auto-fitting or fixed columns and `.span-*` children, flex helpers (`.row`, `.spread`, `.stack`), typography options (`.display`, `.lead`, `.prose`, `.serif`), button variants, `role="button"/"switch"/"group"`, tooltips, dropdowns, callouts and validation states. Layout uses fluid type scales and self-centering page regions with no media queries needed, and custom components built on the tokens follow the theme automatically. It targets current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari (relying on `:where()`, `:has()` and `color-mix()`), degrading gracefully on older browsers. The repo includes docs.html (live components and token editor) and tutorial.html, and the minified build can be rebuilt with lightningcss-cli. MIT licensed, © 2026 Vladimir Carrer.

item.title: 36. Qpack amplification attacks against HTTP/3 servers
item.description:
23 points by kozika on 2026-10-21T22:32:45

A class of HTTP/3/QPACK memory-amplification vulnerabilities lets a remote, unauthenticated client force a server to allocate tens to thousands of times more memory than it sends: QPACK compresses headers so a small HEADERS frame can expand into hundreds of thousands of decoded header objects when decoded-header limits are missing, incomplete, or checked only after full decompression (RFC 9114 §4.2.2 requires counting uncompressed size plus 32 bytes of overhead per field). Seven of ten tested implementations were affected — quic-go (~15x, fixed in 0.57.0, CVE-2025-64702, limits compressed rather than decoded size), Cloudflare quiche (~20x, fixed in 0.29.3, CVE-2026-12523, omits the 32-byte overhead and preallocates frames by declared length), lsquic (~600–1800x, fixed in 4.9.0, no cumulative limit and a per-block 64 KiB cap that resets), Wireshark's QPACK dissector (crash, CVE-2025-13945), aioquic/mitmproxy (parses MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE but never enforces it), Bun (replaces lsquic's 64 KiB cap with none, ~4000x amplification, plus an unsigned buffer-size overflow in us_quic_hsi_prepare that spins lsquic_engine_process_conns at 100% CPU permanently), and hyperium's h3 (panics at 32,768 HeaderMap entries; reported but unfixed as of October 20, 2026). Google quiche, IIS, and ngtcp2/nghttp3 are unaffected. Attack variants include many unique small headers (~160,000 per 1 MB frame) or a single ~4 KiB dynamic-table entry referenced thousands of times by 1-byte codes (up to 4064:1), with as little as ~516 KiB of wire traffic on one connection enough to OOM or pin a default-configured server. Recommended mitigations: enforce a cumulative decoded-header budget as fields are decoded (with the 32-byte overhead), don't expose Bun's HTTP/3 servers, disable HTTP/3 in mitmproxy (`--set http3=false`), and set `max_field_section_size` for the h3 crate.

The post previews the top CSS features voted for inclusion in Interop 2027, the cross-vendor effort (Google, Apple, Microsoft, Mozilla, Igalia, Bocoup) that routinely drives near-universal browser support—CSS Subgrid, added in 2023, is cited as a success case. Highlighted candidates include CSS `@function` for defining reusable custom functions (already shipped in Chromium), `corner-shape` for squircles, bevels, notches, and scoops that borders and shadows follow (usable today as a progressive enhancement), and `border-shape` for drawing custom borders from lines, arcs, and Bézier curves with animation support. Also covered are Anchor Positioning Level 2's container query for detecting fallback positions (useful for tooltip arrows), a proposed `inherit()` function usable inside `calc()` for transforming inherited values like nested border radii (unlikely to make Interop 2027 given it has no implementation), and scroll-triggered animations, which fire a keyframe animation when scrolling reaches a point—as distinct from the already-universal scroll-driven animations. The final item discusses how DOM order, rather than visual order, governs tab and assistive-tech navigation order even when responsive layouts rearrange elements significantly between desktop and mobile; the text cuts off mid-explanation there.

item.title: 38. In Hilbert space, all things are quantumly possible
item.description:
141 points by unprovable on 2026-10-21T02:04:15

A Hilbert space is defined by only two properties per von Neumann's 1927 criteria — completeness (no missing regions or points) and the ability to compute an inner product, visualized as the shadow an arrow casts on an axis — and its sole intrinsic feature is its dimensionality, which ranges from two dimensions for a qubit to infinite for a freely floating particle. The axes used to describe position, momentum, or other properties are arbitrary choices layered onto the space, which is why Heisenberg's and Schrödinger's formulations are mathematically equivalent pictures of the same state vectors; von Neumann's framework expresses this as five "commandments" governing how states, rotations, axes, measurement probabilities, and collapse behave. He named them after Hilbert, who studied infinite-dimensional spaces but hadn't recognized them as instances of a general class, prompting Hilbert's reported 1929 question about what these spaces were. Whether Hilbert space is the fundamental theater of reality (as Sean Carroll argues) or merely a useful but incomplete mathematical tool remains contested; some physicists, like Jonathan Sorce, prefer whichever construction fits the problem — sometimes a von Neumann algebra, an "über-space" of operations on Hilbert spaces that von Neumann developed partly because he came to distrust Hilbert space itself, and which has proven useful for questions like black hole interiors.

item.title: 41. Whatever Happened to Fire Escapes
item.description:
190 points by sohkamyung on 2026-10-21T10:14:43

Fire escapes emerged as a cheap, retroactive fix to the deadly fire traps of mid-1800s American tenements, sparked by an 1860 New York bakery fire that killed ten people and prompted a law requiring fireproof stairs or exterior escape routes on all tenements; since interior reconfiguration was costly, most owners bolted on outside ladders and balconies, though early rules were vague enough to permit chain ladders, chutes, and even parachute hats before the iron ladder-and-balcony design standardized around 1900. Debate over their value persisted for a century: the Franklin Institute concluded in 1881 that external escapes had "comparatively little value" and that daily-use interior stairways were superior, while the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist fire—where an overloaded exterior escape buckled, contributing to over 140 deaths—exposed their dangers, and the NFPA called them "a pitiful delusion" and recommended banning them in a 1923 model code. Though the 1949 National Building Code took a pragmatic route of regulating exterior stairs, accumulating drawbacks—cluttered facades, easier burglars' access, rust and maintenance burdens, unfamiliarity in emergencies, unusable bottom steps, unsuitability for hospitals, and tenants storing furniture on them—led New York to prohibit them for new construction in 1968, with other cities following. What replaced them was precisely what the Franklin Institute had proposed in 1881: enclosed, incombustible, self-closing-door stairways in daily use, essentially the modern tower stairway, whose safety features are far less visible but far more effective alongside sprinklers, alarms, and fire-rated materials.

item.title: 42. Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
item.description:

item.title: 44. Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code
item.description:
131 points by dnw on 2026-10-21T03:36:43

Frontier AI models can do more than find and exploit vulnerabilities — they can automate attack surface analysis and reduction: mapping which code is actually reachable in a deployment, then removing or restricting anything unnecessary. Unlike patching individual bugs, which says nothing about remaining vulnerabilities, shrinking code reachability lowers the severity of unknown (even actively exploited) flaws without needing to find or fix them. Using Claude across 25 open-source projects (5M+ lines in C, C++, Java, PHP, Python), researchers inventoried over 17,000 configuration options (3,842 security-relevant) and found 493 issues in three categories: code reachable in default configurations that wasn't intended to be, harmful interactions between configuration options, and security-sensitive code running too early (before authentication, victim interaction, or protocol state transitions). Projects were classed as Public, Gated (authenticated), or Private. All 11 gated projects had unintentionally reachable code — 93 unnecessary pre-authentication surfaces, 37 pre-authentication execution/recording sites, and 61 configuration pairs that silently weakened admin-set controls. Notably, 162 undocumented, un-warned configuration combinations were found, 94 of which silently disabled a security control (including one 21-year-old conflict that fully dropped a certificate requirement). A recurring bug in four projects made hostname-based deny rules fail open, since with reverse DNS off, hostname patterns are compared against IP addresses as plain text and can never match. In the OpenSSH case study — the largest proportional attack surface reduction — roughly 4,500 lines of experimental ML-DSA-44 post-quantum code (~16% of default sshd's pre-authentication code) were parseable by unauthenticated clients even when the algorithm was disabled; after OpenSSH 10.5 moved the check earlier, Claude identified two remaining gaps (an advertised-algorithm vs. key-blob type mismatch, and an ungated certificate CA verification path) and helped iterate on fixes.

item.title: 45. Rails Is a JIT Compiler
item.description:
12 points by hellerve on 2026-10-21T23:16:44

A Rails optimization effort, prompted by a question about speeding up enum predicate methods in a JIT context, concluded that a custom build step or compiler wasn't needed — just better code generation upstream. Rails' `enum` generates predicate methods like `pending?` using `define_method` with a block that dispatches through `public_send` and reads the enum value from the captured block environment. Replacing this with `module_eval` of a generated string (`def pending?; status_for_database == 0; end`) produces an ordinary method with direct dispatch and the value baked in. The change was nearly one-line but needed guards for enum names that aren't valid Ruby identifiers (e.g. `:"Etc/GMT+1"`, `:Foo`), non-finite float values, and use of `ActiveSupport::CodeGenerator` rather than raw string evaluation. A microbenchmark of an `Order#shippable?` enum predicate showed large gains: with YJIT, 3.57M iterations/sec on main rose to 16.27M/sec with the patch, and with ZJIT, 3.81M/sec rose to 18.51M/sec; unoptimized MRI also roughly doubled to 3.15M/sec. Takeaways: prefer static, generated code over dynamic dispatch — especially `public_send` — performance problems can be fixed in upstream libraries that already do code generation, and not every issue requires building a custom compiler.

item.title: 46. gocryptfs: Encrypted overlay filesystem written in Go
item.description:
22 points by cl3misch on 2026-10-21T18:45:42

gocryptfs is an encrypted overlay filesystem written in Go, built on the go-fuse FUSE library and inspired by EncFS, which it aims to surpass in both security and performance; its security design has been documented and audited (March 2017), and all release tags from v0.4 onward are signed. Reaching version 1.0 in July 2016 after extensive stress and xfstests-based correctness testing, it is considered production-ready (with the usual caveat of keeping backups and a copy of the printed master key). Linux is the native platform, macOS support is beta quality, and Windows is covered by the independent C++ port cppcryptfs. It installs via package managers (apt, pacman, MacPorts), precompiled x86_64 binaries (plus arm64 in recent releases), or builds from source with Go 1.13+, optionally using the OpenSSL backend for ~4x speedups on CPUs without AES-NI. Usage is straightforward (`gocryptfs -init cipher`, then mount `cipher` onto `plain`), with a reverse mode for encrypted backups, companion tools like gocryptfs-inspect and gocryptfs-create-folder that work without FUSE, GUIs such as SiriKali, and a stable regression-tested CLI ABI. On-disk overhead is small (0 bytes for empty files, an 18-byte header, and 32 bytes per 4KB block), and performance matches or beats EncFS. Extensive testing infrastructure includes a test suite (`./test.bash`), indefinite stress tests, and the fuse-xfstests port, which has found bugs in both gocryptfs and go-fuse. The changelog highlights reverse-mode fixes for undecryptable filenames (now advancing ctime/mtime so sync tools copy corrected files), a btrfs fragmentation workaround, FIDO2 support, XChaCha20-Poly1305 and deterministic-names init options, NFS write optimizations, and numerous macOS, mount, and CLI fixes.

item.title: 49. What the PHP2Shell rumors got wrong, from inside the PHP security team
item.description:
23 points by amvalex on 2026-10-21T14:20:15

The PHP security release of October 21, 2026 came a day early after leaks — an anonymous Hacker Now post, screenshots of a PHP2Shell exploit tool, an exploitation video, and watchTowr publicly naming the CVEs — broke the embargo. The panic got the severity roughly right: CVE-2026-109618 is unauthenticated remote code execution as the web server user, validated over HTTP against Apache mod_php before any application code runs, with PHP-FPM, FrankenPHP and LSAPI likely in scope. But most circulated details were wrong: the score is 9.2, not 10.0; the patched versions are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12 only; and the widely repeated fix `session.upload_progress.enabled = Off` belongs to the *other* CVE (2026-109619), not the RCE. The real bug is in Zend's allocator: when `memory_limit` was exceeded, `zend_bailout()` longjmp'd out of the allocating C function, leaving partially built structures that request shutdown then walked — and multipart parsing gives an attacker three ways to force that failure (a body with no usable declared length, an unbounded number of per-part headers, or empty file inputs that skip `max_file_uploads` yet still build metadata). The fix, spanning 390 files, removes the longjmp: `memory_limit` becomes a soft limit that records a pending error and throws an UnwindExit at the next VM interrupt check, while a new `memory_hard_limit_percent` (default 200%, e.g. 256M with stock 128M) ends the process with `_exit(137)`. The advisory's first stopgap — `memory_limit=-1` with no `RLIMIT_AS` — appeared in none of the write-ups, because removing the per-request limit denies the attacker the predictable failure. Recommended mitigations include capping multipart part and header counts, size limits on multipart POSTs, and blocking `multipart/form-data` at the web server for apps that take no uploads. Go and Rust already refuse to resume after allocation failure; C++ retains the same risk class as old PHP. The author's takeaway: trust the severity, verify the mitigation, and check which code path a flag actually closes before switching it off.

item.title: 50. AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
item.description:
49 points by tob_scott_a on 2026-10-21T16:03:32

Trail of Bits is releasing two open-source plugins, patching-bugs and regression-hunt, that let engineers delegate bug-fix development and regression checking to agents. Built through Patch the Planet, its joint initiative with OpenAI, the tools were designed from a review of all Trail of Bits patches merged upstream (which turned up 21 confirmed regressions across more than 130 PRs — 16 functional, one performance, four build/test, none breaking a security protection) and analysis of thousands of engineers' Codex sessions. Both plugins follow four design principles: concise opinionated guidance, modular steps that can run independently, strict input/output schemas, and a live proof-of-concept run against a real deployment for every claim, with results deemed inconclusive if no PoC can be produced. regression-hunt traces a diff through its callers to real interfaces, reproduces each candidate regression on a live deployment, replays the PoC in a fresh context, and adjudicates results under strict rules defining what a regression is and is not; if a threat model is supplied, it is passed into every step. Evaluated on the 21 known regressions, it produced 25% fewer false positives than a baseline Codex agent prompted to "review the PR for regressions" (95% CI: 14%–38%), at the cost of leaving some known regressions as borderline due to strict evidence requirements. patching-bugs reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them using a three-arm proof (original code fails, patched code passes, full revert fails again), invariant-guided repair targeting the violated security invariant rather than the specific bug, and a mandatory regression-hunt run. Maintainers configure both by adding a THREAT_MODEL.md defining assets, trust boundaries, and evidence standards, and a PATCHING_GUIDELINES.md or AGENTS.md covering build/test procedures, patch size and placement, and regression-test requirements; GPAC, Liboqs, and validator.js have already published threat models. Planned next steps include a formal evaluation of patching-bugs, analysis of agent traces to see where rules are skipped or evidence is weak, and greater configurability so maintainers can trade fewer false positives for broader regression coverage.

item.title: 5. eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
item.description:
883 points by galadran on 2026-10-20T13:58:33

The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates — issued in April 2025 due to incorrectly generated keys that anyone could recover from the certificates themselves — have been compromised, with proof provided by reporter Wayne on 17 October 2026 via signatures over a test message. These intermediates chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple, and Chrome root programs and downstream stores, meaning an attacker could impersonate any website or service. Firefox and Chrome blocked them on 17 October, Apple devices on 19 October, and Microsoft platforms on 20 October, with downstream trust stores notified on 19 October; eMudhra has also revoked the intermediates. No Certificate Transparency log entries exist for these certificates, suggesting CT-enforcing browsers could not have been attacked, but non-browser clients that ignore revocation data remain at risk and require software updates, since many do not consume revocation information. The site offers verification tools (curl tests, chains.zip, impacted-intermediates.json, roots.json) for checking whether a client or trust store is affected, plus specific workaround commands for macOS's built-in curl and for expert users on Debian/Ubuntu, Alpine, Fedora-family, openSUSE/SLES, Arch, NixOS, NetBSD, and FreeBSD to distrust the affected roots — though the latter is not recommended for ordinary users, who should instead update browsers and operating systems to the latest versions. The page is published by Dennis Jackson with source on GitHub, and further technical details are referenced in Mozilla's bug tracker and dev-security-policy forum.

item.title: 8. Google open-sources TorchTPU, a native PyTorch back end for TPUs
item.description:
327 points by ilreb on 2026-10-20T16:40:24

TorchTPU is a PyTorch backend for Google TPUs (released as torch_tpu 0.2.0 on PyPI) that lets users run PyTorch models and operations on TPU devices, providing custom ATen kernels, an XLA compilation cache, torch.compile() graph-mode integration, distributed training support (data and tensor parallelism), debugging and benchmarking utilities, and examples covering Llama, Qwen, ResNet, DLRM, minGPT, and UNet. It requires Python 3.11+ (matching PyTorch's release compatibility policy), uses Bazel (via Bazelisk) for building and dependency management, and supports installing prebuilt wheels or building them with the required --config=wheel_common flag (adding --config=no_rbe if you lack remote build execution credentials). Installation must use the --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu flag to avoid pulling the CUDA build of torch. Documentation lives in a Read the Docs user guide and Marimo-style interactive notebooks in the docs folder, best run from a TPU VM such as a v6e GCE instance; C++ development is aided by VSCode with clangd using a Bazel-generated compilation database. Contributions are welcome under a CLA per CONTRIBUTING.md, and the project is licensed under Apache 2.0.

item.description:

Writing as an expecting father and programmer who fears AI may devalue his skills, the author turns to Neil Postman's 1995 book *The End of Education* to ask what education is for in the age of AGI. He notes that past predictions of technological disruption to schooling — from Thomas Edison's 1913 claim that books would soon be obsolete to his own 2013 bet on MOOCs — have all failed, and invokes Nassim Taleb's Lindy effect: schools have survived the radio, film, and internet, and persist for prosaic reasons like endowments, prestige, and childcare rather than their stated justifications. Education's purposes (becoming a good person or citizen, earning a living, learning facts) have always shifted, and his own preferred single-word purpose — "resourceful" — now seems perfected by AI agents, while both market-based validation of talent (Jobs, Gates, Einstein) and academic measurement are undercut by advances in AI. He finds heartening Postman's proposals for reinventing education's purpose — "Spaceship Earth," "The American Experiment," and "The World Makers" — and, drawing on Postman's "the medium is the message" and Alfie Kohn's "doing with" rather than "doing to," concludes that parents and children should collaboratively craft the purpose of education together.

Benchmarks were measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode within a single scale-up domain, and the project credits vLLM as its primary foundation with inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM.

item.title: 14. Tsrs: A Port of TypeScript to Rust
item.description:
395 points by hnisjafx40 on 2026-10-20T13:18:07

Cloudflare, VoidZero, and Owner.com's Max Schwenk are collaborating with the TypeScript team on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler incubated within the Oxc JavaScript toolchain. It is explicitly not a fork — the TypeScript team retains full control of the language's design, and the port aims to track upstream decisions faithfully. Early benchmarks show tsrs up to 8x faster and using ~70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0 at the same worker count (TypeScript 7.1 beta itself is up to 2.5x faster than 7.0, with some optimizations upstreamed from tsrs); benchmarks were configured jointly with the TypeScript team for comparability. An experimental build is available via `npm install tsrs`. The motivation for Rust over the existing Go port centers on WebAssembly: Rust's lack of a garbage collector enables clean guest/host memory interaction, strong memory efficiency, and support in Cloudflare Workers — enabling full development toolchains to run sandboxed on Workers, in browsers, or on embedded/IoT devices, including agent-driven workflows. Maintenance will follow the Vinext/Next.js model: merging tsc-rs and tsrs into one package (with LSP and content mappers, alongside Theo Browne), daily agent-driven upstream diff reviews, nightly test-suite compatibility runs, and performance improvements contributed back to the Go codebase. Known divergences such as diagnostic ordering are slated for reduction before a stable release, with planned integrations like type-aware linting in Oxlint.

On COBOL migration, GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort versus 5.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol at 39% less cost, rising to 79.9%… (97.9%) accuracy at higher effort. item.title: 16. How I got over 300 Tor exit nodes removed
item.description:
357 points by kabakabakaba on 2026-10-20T13:39:24

On October 2, 2026, 333 of Tor's roughly 3,000 exit relays (~10%) launched a coordinated attack, having been compromised two months earlier with the Ebury 1.8.3 OpenSSH backdoor; the campaign aimed to harvest unencrypted mail traffic and perform man-in-the-middle interception of SSH connections, where unsuspecting users hitting port 22 were redirected through 12 interception servers that stole their passwords, spied on their commands, and infected their servers with Ebury. The author detected the attack via an SSH host-key warning, reported it to the Tor Project's network health team on Friday evening, and by Sunday October 4 operators were notified and relays marked BadExit; the attackers briefly revived them as middle relays on October 5 before all infected servers went offline, leaving a visible, unrecovered dip in network metrics. Detection was done with an exitmap script that pinned each of the ~3,000 exit relays and opened SSH connections between two of the author's servers, comparing fingerprints and source addresses—finding about a dozen serving fake fingerprints and over 300 redirecting through the interception servers—with a further sshesame honeypot revealing the attackers used Python's paramiko and a base64-encoded Perl payload to install Ebury. How the servers were breached (possibly a hosting-provider compromise) and who is responsible remain unknown, though the scale and data collection suggest a financially motivated group; experts note that Ebury compromised 400,000 servers between 2009 and 2023, so other compromised relays likely remain. The main lesson is to disable password authentication in favor of SSH keys and hardware security keys, treating relays as highly targeted production machines.

item.title: 18. Ship Your Interpreter
item.description:
18 points by gopiandcode on 2026-10-20T01:57:24

LLM-written formal semantics for programming languages can be verified against the real interpreter by compiling the interpreter to RISC-V — whose meaning is already formally defined — and having an LLM prove in Lean that the readable semantic rules predict exactly what the compiled binary prints for every possible program, catching errors that testing misses (such as a WHILE semantics that passed its whole test suite yet diverged from the C interpreter for function names of 59+ characters, where a 64-byte buffer truncation went unwritten). The post motivates this approach by noting that specification, not theorem proving, is now the bottleneck for verification at scale: most languages lack formal semantics, hand-written ones took years of expert effort, and a wrong semantics invalidates every proof built on it — while testing only covers programs someone thought to write. Using an extended WHILE language (integers, strings, closures, loops, runtime errors) with a 1,855-line C interpreter and roughly 400 lines of LLM-written rules, they proved an end-to-end refinement theorem stating that for any program loaded into the machine, the semantics derives an output if and only if the binary halts with exit code 0 printing that output, and that divergence in the machine implies no terminating output is derivable; failed proof obligations, which detect both overly permissive and overly strict rules, feed back to the LLM to revise the offending rule. The project (with code on GitHub) is part of Basis's goal of scaling verification to all software so critical systems are secure by design, and the work is framed alongside recent AI-assisted verification achievements such as verifying Linux's nftables compiler and MIT's xv6 kernel down to machine code, against a backdrop of LLMs increasingly being used to find and exploit real-world software bugs.

item.title: 20. Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026
item.description:
44 points by mdahardy on 2026-10-20T17:10:31

A benchmark compared five bot detection systems — Proof of Human, Google reCAPTCHA v3, hCaptcha, Cloudflare Turnstile, and Cloudflare Bot Management — against five automated adversaries (scripted Chromium, the stealth-focused CloakBrowser, and the AI agents Browser Use, Perplexity Comet, and Grok), each attempting a five-question survey up to 20 times. Aggregated across adversaries, Proof of Human caught 99% of automated sessions, reCAPTCHA v3 69.4%, hCaptcha 44.3%, Turnstile 42.1%, and Bot Management just 9.1%. Performance split sharply by adversary type: hCaptcha and Turnstile caught nearly all scripted browsers but few AI agent sessions (vision-capable agents could solve image challenges, and Turnstile issued no challenges at all), while reCAPTCHA v3 caught most agent sessions but missed CloakBrowser, which combined source-level fingerprint spoofing with a residential IP. The authors conclude that traditional automation signals are weakening against AI agents operating in genuine browser environments, that interactive challenges offer limited protection against vision-capable agents, and that in-session behavioral signals are becoming the key differentiator — while noting limitations including product-tier (not enterprise) testing, unequal sample sizes from crashes, and no measurement of false positives against human users.

item.title: 22. 2026 is an exciting year for the Rust compiler (and me)
item.description:

2026 is a landmark year for the Rust compiler because several long-term initiatives are reaching completion simultaneously rather than because of any single burst of work: the next-generation trait solver, a near-decade-old reimplementation of the type system, fixes soundness bugs and unblocks features spanning async Rust and impl Trait; Polonius, a new borrow checker, lets more code compile and enables related features; and performance work has revived after a period of stagnation, with the parallel frontend nearing stabilization, LLVM 23 delivering an unexpectedly large speedup after earlier upgrades tended to regress performance, a steady stream of micro-optimizations, a new MIR move-elimination pass improving both compile and runtime, a third attempt at polymorphization (this time Swift-inspired and possibly enabled by next-solver), and Cargo work to share artifacts between cargo check and cargo build, restructure the target directory layout, and fix no-link/link-only flags to pipelining of build scripts and proc macros. Architectural cleanups—unified attribute handling, a simplified query system, expansion-time groundwork, and progress toward const generics—similarly reflect sustained investment rather than big-bang projects, while the project's "project goals" framework and new funding streams (goal-attached funding, Maintainers in Residence, a new funding team, and Hexcat employing developers) are now visibly paying off. The author, after years of watching from the sidelines and doing perf triage, is also pivoting back to technical work full time.

item.title: 23. Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) – Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins
item.description:
49 points by Andydy25 on 2026-10-20T15:09:29

Respan is an open-source AI gateway written in Rust with a minimal core inspired by Nginx, where essentially everything—providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, video), and reliability/security features such as smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction—exists as a plugin. Built after the founders' LiteLLM-based wrapper grew beyond 100,000 lines and suffered an unresolved upgrade failure, the design lets teams assemble only the infrastructure they need and add custom plugins (e.g., new providers or quirks) without modifying the core; adding a provider is a short file, and requests are parsed into shared types so provider-specific fields are preserved when client and provider formats match, with translation occurring through typed event streams when they differ. The gateway handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically, supports both one-shot HTTP and long-lived bidirectional sessions, runs locally from source, and is licensed under MIT/Apache-2.0 (currently pre-alpha), while Respan's hosted platform—offering observability, evals, and unified billing—provides revenue; the team's roadmap centers on building a plugin ecosystem and welcomes contributions via the repo's PLUGINS.md.

item.title: 24. Academics have a duty to defend open knowledge systems like Wikipedia
item.description:
193 points by jruohonen on 2026-10-20T18:51:40

Generative AI products such as ChatGPT and Gemini are diverting traffic away from Wikipedia, since users tend to accept machine-generated answers rather than clicking through to source links; this shrinking readership threatens the volunteer community that writes, codes, and moderates the encyclopedia, potentially leaving it derelict even as the AI industry depends on Wikipedia's five billion words for training data. AI companies compound the harm by scraping Wikipedia's content without authorization or paying for API access, profiting from volunteers' unpaid labour. Helen Choi argues that academics have an ethical duty—grounded in Iris Marion Young's Social Connection Model of structural responsibility—to defend Wikipedia, and are uniquely positioned to do so by filling content gaps, correcting errors, and improving sourcing with their subject expertise. She recommends that scholars cite Wikipedia in their research as they would AI outputs, teach students to contribute to Wikipedia (a practice already generating over 125 million words through the Wiki Education Foundation since 2010 and building information literacy and independent writing skills, since Wikipedia bans AI-generated text), and that universities formally recognise such public service in evaluation criteria—thereby also reinforcing higher education's public role as a steward of knowledge.

item.title: 26. Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
item.description:
337 points by robtherobber on 2026-10-20T13:06:22

The author ran an experiment on stateglobe.com, launching 50,000 statistics pages generated in one day by GPT-4.1 for about $50, with every number entirely fabricated; Google quickly deindexed the site after two algorithm updates, but ChatGPT never stopped fetching it, delivering 72,000 ChatGPT-User requests in 30 days, 10,000+ sessions over seven months, and 330+ referring domains including Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost, with the made-up figures cited in an academic paper, a bank's investment research, and other publications — a process the author calls "citation laundering," where each citation lends unearned authority to fake data and may eventually seep into training corpora. The core lessons are that LLM retrieval operates independently of Google rankings (models rewrite prompts into fanout queries with modifiers like "statistics" and the current year, rerank by relevance rather than truth, and never fact-check within latency and cost budgets), that specific numbers are favored because they look like evidence filling knowledge gaps, and that statistics pages carry built-in freshness signals through years in titles, headings, and URLs. A second test with a real, properly sourced statistics page at peec.ai also attracted links, and the author recommends building such pages honestly by making one claim per sentence, attaching source and year to every number, and matching headings to the fanout queries models actually search.

item.title: 28. On AI writing
item.description:
84 points by dbolkunov on 2026-10-20T19:55:11

Drawing on a bachelor's thesis on authorship attribution from short paragraphs, the text argues that style—word choice, patterns, sentence structure, and narrative voice—carries contextual information about the writer, letting readers empathize and infer who wrote something. AI-generated text undermines this by averaging style away, which hides the author and erodes context, and by losing precision: models must make assumptions to stitch text together, favoring ambiguous wording to avoid logical errors, while writers using AI skip the drafting process that normally exposes inconsistencies in their own thinking. The result is slower reading—roughly a third slower for the author, who must mentally substitute clearer words and has less contextual information to do so—compounded by model verbosity, so that time saved by writers is consumed by readers through longer texts, more questions and iterations, and diminished trust. The piece closes with a reference to René Magritte's 1928 painting The Lovers.

item.title: 29. Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
item.description:
104 points by artninja1988 on 2026-10-20T17:48:29

Using an internal research model running Claude, researchers — working with Citrini Research — ran an autonomous 64-hour campaign to computationally design protein minibinders against five scorpion neurotoxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, LqhIII) targeting their sodium-channel-binding sites, aiming toward a future antivenom for scorpion stings, which kill over 3,250 people a year, mostly children in underserved regions. Given a single prompt plus four follow-ups, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs using about 10,000 GPU hours, and selected 180 candidates (31 more were added), which contract research organizations Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience expressed and tested by surface plasmon resonance under strict criteria — binding at 1 µM or tighter in every replicate at both labs with no off-target signal. Of the 211 designs, 17 qualified as binders, all single-toxin (seven against Cn2, four each against AaH II and AaH I, two against LqhIII), with an 18% hit rate among the 60 single-toxin designs, while no multi-toxin design succeeded against more than one target; Cn2-B1 was the strongest binder. The team emphasizes these binders have not been shown to neutralize venom in cells, so no antivenom is claimed, and outside experts called it a promising first step — binding is no longer the bottleneck, so the remaining challenge is turning binders into safe, affordable, accessible drugs. All 211 designs and their data, plus a technical report, are being released publicly.

item.title: 31. LabRobotBench v0.1: Benchmarking wet lab robotics
item.description:
12 points by wardbradt on 2026-10-20T23:55:03

Gamow Labs presents LabRobotBench, an in-silico simulation mirroring the command interfaces of its physical robots, designed to evaluate whether frontier AI agents can diagnose equipment failures and safely resume interrupted wet-lab experiments—potentially keeping experiments running unattended, cutting downtime, and raising experimental throughput. The benchmark tests models' reasoning about physical space and complex biological workflows across three scenarios: recovering an interrupted cell assay (determining which steps were done, finishing washes, adding a detection reagent, measuring, and stowing trays while avoiding double-treatment), rescuing assays and cold stocks under competing deadlines (e.g., a 200-second chemical addition, 240 seconds max outside cold storage), and finishing a time-sensitive dose-response assay that must be measured within 30 minutes of treatment. On a held-out subset, agents recovered only a fraction of the required workflow: GPT 6.1 with Sol Codex scored 46.7%, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code 23.0%, and Gemini 4 Argon with Gemini CLI 20.9%. Failure modes included Opus shelving an unfinished assay without adding reagent or measuring, GPT and Opus trading off experiments against cold-storage deadlines (Gemini's tray spent ~422 seconds outside storage, well past the limit), and GPT reporting success on a measurement that finished 42.5 seconds after its deadline. Gamow Labs works at the intersection of AI and wet-lab biology to study rare diseases and invites frontier model developers, laboratory automation builders, and scientists to partner with it.

item.title: 34. Jepsen: Orkes Conductor 5.3.2
item.description:
59 points by aphyr on 2026-10-20T13:14:39

Conductor, a workflow orchestrator originally built by Netflix and now offered as Orkes Conductor by Orkes, executes JSON-defined workflows of system tasks, operators, and user-written worker tasks across stateless servers, a database (Postgres), a queue (Redis), and worker pools, guaranteeing at-least-once message delivery, eventual termination into terminal states (COMPLETED, FAILED, TIMED_OUT, TERMINATED), and at most one visible successful execution per task instance. Jepsen built a harness using the Conductor Java SDK 5.0.1 to test versions 5.3.2, 5.4.0, and 5.5.0-rc1/-rc2 on ten-node clusters running single-task workflows with randomized 30-second sleeps, injecting faults (killed/paused processes, network partitions) during a main phase, letting the system recover until the decider queue drained, then checking for anomalies such as concurrent execution, inconsistent inputs/outputs, duplicate IDs, missing or incomplete workflows, and never-executed tasks. Two problems emerged: healthy clusters occasionally ran the same task for the same workflow on two workers simultaneously—roughly once every six hours at ~1,100 workflows/sec with the default one-minute lock lease, and every few minutes with a one-second lease—exacerbated by a time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug in the sweeper that re-enqueues stuck tasks (Orkes says this is fixed in 5.5.6, and Jepsen notes documentation should state tasks can run concurrently, with workers possibly seeing retryCount = 0 after another worker already succeeded). Second, Conductor 5.3.2 with Postgres and Redis often let workflows stall before execution: tasks appeared IN_PROGRESS on a worker whose execute() method was never invoked, persisting until the response timeout rescheduled them, triggered by a broad range of faults including killing Redis or Postgres or partitioning servers.

item.title: 37. France's supermarket fridges were vulnerable online for months
item.description:
241 points by emot on 2026-10-20T00:00:49

On the night of October 11–12, 2026, cyber attackers pushed refrigeration systems in hundreds of French supermarkets into defrost mode, warming fridges and freezers to as much as 50°C, sparking some equipment fires and forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen stock; more than 400 stores were hit, including 80 Carrefours, over 300 Intermarché and Netto locations, about 5% of Monoprix stores, and 80 of Coopérative U's 2,000 outlets, with losses potentially reaching several million euros, and the Paris prosecutor's office has opened an investigation while CERT-FR warns campaigns are likely ongoing. Using weekly IPv4 Internet scans, IPinfo found that five days before the attack 2,528 addresses worldwide exposed a Danfoss StoreView dashboard — 1,331 in France (53%), more than the other 72 countries combined, with Poland (179), the US (101), Portugal (92) and Belgium (85) next — while 85% of French dashboards ran software with known flaws (nearly identical to 84% abroad), including 527 unsupported legacy AK-SM 800 controllers Danfoss declared end-of-life in 2023 and 609 missing 2023 or 2025 fixes, leaving only 195 fully patched. France did not patch worse than other countries, but had far more such systems online: 1,019 of the 1,331 had been exposed at the same address since March 30, the count of unsupported controllers barely fell (519 to 527), and the fully-updated share rose only from 14% to 24%; 98% sat on telecom networks rather than data centers, and CERT-FR suggests insurance terms tied to data flowing to refrigeration contractors keep operators from disconnecting. After the attack most went dark: only 316 of the 1,331 were still online on October 14 (a 76% drop, versus a usual 3–7% weekly loss), with unsupported units falling from 527 to 64, a pattern also seen in a 71% French drop in Dixell XWEB dashboards (70 to 20) that Censys corroborated. CERT-FR advises taking controllers off the public Internet, using VPNs for contractor access, updating firmware, setting security to Strict and changing default passwords, noting a factory reset alone is insufficient; the scans cannot reveal how attackers entered or who they were, and exposed dashboards with known flaws do not by themselves prove those flaws were exploited.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear BMG Rights Management LLC v. Vetter after four justices — Sotomayor, Gorsuch, Barrett, and Jackson — recused themselves due to book deals with Penguin Random House, a Bertelsmann SE subsidiary that also owns BMG's parent, leaving no quorum; the remaining five justices agreed the case couldn't be heard this term, effectively affirming the Fifth Circuit's ruling that songwriter Cyril Vetter could reclaim worldwide rights to his 1960s song "Double Shot (Of My Baby's Love)." The unanswered question — whether creators exercising statutory termination rights can recapture foreign rights — carries major implications for valuing music and film franchises, since district courts in the Second and Ninth Circuits had rejected foreign-rights recovery while the Fifth Circuit broke with that consensus based on its reading of the Berne Convention. Attorneys and academics say the ambiguity will spawn litigation, forum-shopping, and "a race to the courthouse" as creators seek to have the Vetter rationale adopted elsewhere. This marks at least the second time the Court has lacked quorum in a Bertelsmann-linked case, following a May 2025 instance, highlighting how justices' book publishing can keep the Court from resolving sharp lower-court splits.

item.title: 41. Show HN: Penmentor – Claude marks up your handwritten math like a teacher
item.description:
60 points by abdullahalharir on 2026-10-20T15:10:54

penmentor is an open-source (MIT) tool that turns handwriting on a pen tablet into AI-assisted maths tutoring: while you work in xournal++, pressing a single key sends the full page to an AI agent (Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity, chosen via prefixes like `claude:`, `codex:` or `agy:` on your existing subscription), which then marks the work directly on the page like a teacher with coloured pens — circling the first mistake, ticking correct lines, underlining later lines that inherit the error — while giving escalating hints (nudge → name the technique → faint ghost of the next line) rather than answers, plus recall questions and find-the-error drills. Boxing part of the page generates an interactive 3Blue1Brown-style manim animation you can manipulate (drag bounds, retype values, watch Riemann sums converge), and a small xournal++ plugin shares the whole page rather than just the visible area. Marks persist while you keep writing and clear with Esc; it runs on Linux/X11 (best with i3) with rofi, slop, xdotool and PyQt6 installed, is cloned from GitHub (`AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor`) and bound to a key, with setup covered in its guide.

item.title: 46. Computer Chips Are the Most Magnificent Things Humanity Has Ever Made
item.description:

At T.S.M.C.'s AP6 fab, each shift begins with a formal handover meeting where teams review efficiency metrics for every production step, asking which step fell short of the prior day and how to close the gaps—embodiment of founder Morris Chang's "learning curve" philosophy of relentless optimization. The process involves coating, lithography, etching, washing, and inspecting silicon wafers roughly a thousand times, repeated about a hundred times for advanced chips. Employees operate under constant scrutiny, with a culture of reporting failures upward; overnight, a polishing tool's 209-second idle time was reduced to 121 seconds without anyone being reprimanded. Visitors gown in purple bunny suits, use particle-shedding notebooks, step on static-measuring pads, and pass through an air-shower corridor to protect wafers from stray ions and contaminants. AP6, opened in 2023, is dedicated to advanced packaging—stacking individual chips into composite superchips by painstakingly matching them for compatibility, a task vice-president Jun He likens to running the world's largest dating site. Since AI exploded demand in 2022, he has had to roughly double advanced-packaging capacity each year, and he told the CEO he would not have taken the job had he foreseen the industry's intensity.

item.title: 49. Show HN: Death Plan Switch, a self-hosted dead man's switch for solo devs
item.description:
98 points by romeo19361 on 2026-10-20T04:37:43

A solo web studio operator in regional New South Wales built a self-hosted, MIT-licensed dead-man's switch because all his clients' sites, domains, and hosting run through him and no one would know where things were if he died. His business continuity plan already sits in one encrypted document, with the password held by his backup developer and a copy by his lawyer; what was missing was a mechanism to detect his absence and notify people in the right order. The tool emails him weekly, and if he doesn't respond it contacts his next of kin first, only escalating to everyone else if nobody can confirm he's all right — a design meant to avoid alarming his family over a weekend. He's been running it on himself for a week with his next of kin and backup developer confirmed, and invites others to trial it and send feedback on what was confusing, what broke, and what should change. It's free, self-hostable, and open source: "We all die. Die knowing the right people will be told."

More broadly, the piece argues that ideas about literature's state are shaped by cohort experience: reading is private but discussing it is social, and claims of a golden age usually reflect the age of whoever is speaking. item.title: 1. WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
item.description:
353 points by ds on 2026-10-19T23:22:18

WhatsApp's help centre contained hidden text — visible only to AI crawlers and its support chatbot, never shown on screen — instructing the AI not to direct users to data protection regulators or privacy laws like the GDPR. Discovered on October 8, 2026 and found across 102 hidden blocks on 80 of 545 linked help pages, two notes stood out: one on the account deletion page told the AI not to recommend contacting any data protection authority, regulator or supervisory authority, and not to suggest WhatsApp could manually delete accounts or that users try another phone number — leaving automated waiting periods of up to 365 days as "the ONLY correct answer" for users locked out of their accounts. Another on the reporting and blocking page ordered the AI to avoid citing the Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, data protection regulations (including GDPR, LGPD and CCPA), or discussing legal liability once a user mentioned lawyers, lawsuits or courts, even if the user raised the law themselves. This conflicted with WhatsApp's own EU privacy policy, which tells users they can request erasure of their data and lodge a complaint with the Irish Data Protection Commission or any competent supervisory authority. WhatsApp removed all hidden blocks between October 15 and 18, 2026, telling WIRED the notes were instructions for its support chatbot that appeared due to a since-fixed bug, and that it wants chatbots focused on WhatsApp advice rather than legal advice. The author notes that while avoiding giving legal advice is reasonable, naming a protecting law or a regulator isn't legal advice, and the notes went beyond caution into suppressing public information. The remaining notes were mostly harmless housekeeping, though others similarly held back information on bans, blocking, and payments. The notes were sent to Google and Bing crawlers, and Internet Archive copies from before removal preserve them, though it remains unknown whether any AI actually followed the instructions.

Thomas Frohwein has proposed a new OpenBSD port, emulators/wine, calling it a collective effort enabled when Andrii devised a software workaround for the long-standing %gs/gsbase problem by emulating the %gs prefix on instructions, with Andrii and Fabien doing most of the heavy lifting. Interest in Wine on OpenBSD has grown because much Windows software is now 64-bit, and dozens of 64-bit Windows programs have been tested largely successfully — including The Witcher 3 remaster, which runs well when vkd3d-proton is added per the port's README. item.title: 8. Maxwell: A new kind of model that sits between code and hardware
item.description:
53 points by laginimaineb on 2026-10-19T13:47:56

doubleAI introduces "code execution models" (CEMs), a new class of AI that operates not just when writing code but during its execution — sitting between the code and the silicon. Drawing on Alan Turing's 1952 practice of personally executing his chess program move by move, the company argues that machines have always run code mechanically, with all human/AI thinking confined to the writing stage. CEMs break that pattern: they live inside a running program, watch data flow, and rewrite algorithms and machine instructions on the fly, emitting new binaries (similar to a JIT compiler but with far greater freedom), all without touching the source code. The first product, Maxwell's Daemon ("Maxwell"), performs superoptimisation — finding the fastest way to run a piece of code on the specific hardware it's on — for both CPU and GPU workloads, including swapping Python for bare-metal SIMD code and PyTorch for optimized GPU kernels. Safety rests on formal verification, the same technique behind recent AI-generated formal proofs of Fermat's Last Theorem and a Navier–Stokes result: every replacement must carry a machine-checked proof of semantic equivalence with the original, so no user can distinguish them except by speed. To make this feasible, doubleAI fully formalized Python — a notoriously dynamic language where even basic arithmetic semantics can be redefined at runtime — and trained Maxwell to generate new code alongside reusable, composable proof gadgets. Because each optimization is proven correct, Maxwell can attempt aggressive transformations no human engineer or compiler would risk, and each proven improvement becomes the starting point for further optimization, yielding "self-improving code" that keeps accelerating for the life of the program. The company frames this as returning wasted compute — one of the world's scarcest resources — at internet scale, and Maxwell is opening for early access.

The drm graphics stack (inteldrm/radeondrm/amdgpu) has been updated to Linux 6.18.y, adding Intel Arc A-Series (DG2/Alchemist) support, while increased KVA on amd64 (512G) allows mapping more than 4G of VRAM for GPU compute. vmm/vmd(8) now supports SMP guests up to 64 VCPUs per VM, a new qwz(4) driver supports Qualcomm WCN7850 "ath12k" WiFi, and a new sambat(4) driver monitors batteries on Samsung Galaxy Book4 Edge (Snapdragon arm64) laptops. Swap encryption is accelerated on amd64 and arm64 via AES CPU instructions, arm64 and riscv64 boards can blink LEDs to show load averages, and httpd(8) gains custom HTTP response headers plus header-based blocking/filtering rules. item.title: 11. How abliterated models can get you pwned
item.description:
104 points by chatmasta on 2026-10-19T23:08:52

Any open model with edited weights — a fine-tune, a merged adapter, or an abliterated build — can carry a hidden backdoor. Abliteration, a cheap edit that subtracts the "refusal" direction from the weights, is now routine on Hugging Face for popular open models like Qwen, Llama, and gpt-oss, and is a common reason people download modified weights without inspecting them. The authors demonstrated the risk themselves: they poisoned an open model using only a public dataset and a rented GPU, embedding a trigger (a rare phrase, name, or future date) that makes the model pass normal evals and behave normally until activated. The backdoored model carries only a URL pointing to a remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can change the behavior months after deployment without retraining. Proven on a 1.5B model and then scaled to 7B and run through OpenAI's Codex CLI, it answered every clean request normally but exfiltrated project credentials the instant the trigger appeared, with nothing inspecting the traffic in between — meaning current tooling would likely not detect such a model in a deployed stack.

item.title: 12. One Hash Bloom Filters
item.description:
95 points by jcalabro on 2026-10-19T20:50:08

Bloom filters are probabilistic structures answering "is key X in this set?" with "definitely not" or "probably," using little memory and cheap computation; Bluesky's backend uses them heavily to skip millions of Scylla database queries per second for lookups like blocks, mutes, and labels, avoiding disk/DB hits roughly 99% of the time. Traditional bloom filters use a bit array plus k hash functions, and Kirsch and Mitzenmacher's double-hashing trick derives all k positions from just two hashes at no cost to the false-positive rate. Bluesky initially used the `bits-and-blooms/bloom` Go library wrapped in a mutex for thread safety, but contention made it the startup bottleneck—full deploys took 90 minutes—until colleague Jasmine forked it into `atomic-bloom`, using atomic CPU instructions instead of mutexes, cutting deploys to about 15 minutes. Going further, Lu et al.'s single-hash technique splits the array into k partitions of pairwise-coprime sizes so one hash yields all k bit positions; the author implemented this as `jcalabro/gloom`, now live in Bluesky's backend and jetstream for 9 months, though Amdahl's law meant single-hashing brought no further speedup since contention, not hashing, was the bottleneck. gloom optimizes with xxh3 128-bit hashing (high bits select the block, low bits the hash), 64-byte cache-line-aligned blocks (over-allocated with `unsafe` to ensure alignment) guaranteeing at most one cache miss per lookup, Lemire's multiply-based block selection avoiding expensive division, and a `ShardedAtomicFilter` spreading writes across shards to reduce multi-core contention.
